articles.title: Ukraine’s Brave1 says it can down Russia’s Banderol missiles with  cruising speed 650 km/h for less than what they cost, and has destroyed at least four
articles.body:
Ukraine says it has found a way to shoot down Russia's Banderol jet missiles for less than the missiles themselves cost. A system from a developer in the Brave1 defense-tech cluster has already destroyed at least four of them, Brave1 said, releasing video of the intercepts.
The point is the price tag, not the kills. The Banderol is built to be cheap for Russia and expensive for Ukraine to stop, forcing Kyiv to spend scarce, costly air-defense missiles on a low-cost weapon. A counter that costs less than the target flips that math back against Russia.
A cluster developer downs four Banderols
The footage Brave1 shared shows a defender in the cluster hitting at least four Banderol missiles.
"The cost of interception is substantially cheaper than the cost of the drone-missiles themselves," the cluster said.
It added that several products capable of countering the Banderol now exist, and that it is scaling the ones that work.
Kronshtadt built the missile to bleed defenses
The S8000 Banderol is a hybrid of a cruise missile and a jet-powered attack drone, made by the sanctioned Russian firm Kronshtadt, which also builds the Orion reconnaissance drone that launches it. It flies at a cruising speed of 520 to 560 km/h and up to 650 km/h at full throttle, and carries a 114.3-kilogram fragmentation-high-explosive warhead, of which 49.5 kilograms is explosive.
The design is built for cheap mass production: it runs on a Chinese hobby turbojet sold online for about $16,000, and Ukrainian media have put the cost of a single Banderol near $100,000, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Russia has used it to strike Odesa, Kharkiv, Kyiv, and Black Sea ports.
Ukraine keeps finding cheap answers
Brave1's system is the newest in a pattern of low-cost counters. In July, Ukrainian troops downed Banderols with Swedish Bofors L70 anti-aircraft guns designed in the late 1940s. The task now is to turn scattered successes into enough deployed systems to blunt a weapon Russia is firing in growing numbers, which is what Brave1 says it is racing to do.

articles.title: 175 Targets Down, But Ballistic Missiles Still Get Through
articles.body:
Ukraine’s air defenses intercepted 175 Russian aerial targets overnight, but President Volodymyr Zelensky said ballistic missiles remain a major challenge as Kyiv steps up efforts to secure additional interceptors and develop its FREYJA anti-ballistic system.
In a Telegram post on Tuesday, Sept. 8, Zelensky said the overnight Russian attack combined ballistic and cruise missiles, anti-ship missiles and Shahed drones, in what he described as a complex assault designed to inflict maximum damage.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Despite very good results with cruise missiles, it is especially difficult with ballistics,” Zelensky said, adding that Ukraine continues to need additional interceptors.
He said Ukraine had already raised the issue with its US and European partners.
“We have already talked about this with the Americans and Europeans, and there will be more meetings, in particular today, with representatives of states and companies that can help with supplies and with our FREYJA anti-ballistic system,” Zelensky said.
“Thank you to all our partners who make air defense assistance to Ukraine a priority. This directly means saving people’s lives,” he added.
Russian attack causes damage across Ukraine
The overnight attack targeted Kyiv and several other Ukrainian regions.
In Kyiv and the surrounding region, emergency crews continued working on Tuesday to clear the aftermath. Zelensky said residential buildings and other civilian infrastructure sustained significant damage.
A Tale Of Two Cities
Thirteen people were rescued by State Emergency Service (DSNS) workers, while 10 people in Kyiv were reported injured. Two people were killed, Zelensky said.
Critical infrastructure was also targeted in the Kyiv region.
In the Odesa region, a regular market was struck. Additionally, two people were wounded in Kharkiv, where an apartment building was damaged.
In the Sumy region, Russian forces attacked a diesel locomotive of the Kyiv-Sumy train at a railway station. No one was injured, but an evacuation was underway, Zelensky said.
Strikes were also reported in Zaporizhzhia and the Dnipropetrovsk regions.
Failed pause
Russia’s three-day pause on strikes against Kyiv appeared to unravel hours before its stated deadline on Monday, as Russian drones were detected over the capital while US envoys were still in Kyiv seeking to revive peace talks.
On Monday, at 8:45 p.m, Ukraine’s Air Force warned of a Russian jet-powered drone over Kyiv and several others approaching the capital – more than three hours before Moscow’s stated 11:59 p.m. deadline.
The attacks intensified overnight, with explosions heard across Kyiv at around 3:30 a.m. on Tuesday after authorities issued an air raid alert and warned of a missile threat.
Russian drones also struck the Boryspil and Fastiv districts of the Kyiv region. Fires broke out at industrial facilities in Boryspil, seven trucks were destroyed, and a logistics complex was hit twice, according to Ukraine’s DSNS.
Limited ceasefire
Russian state news agency TASS reported that the three-day suspension ordered by President Vladimir Putin had expired. Russian accounts said the pause began at midnight between Friday and Saturday and was to last until 11:59 p.m. on Monday.
The halt was limited largely to Kyiv and Moscow rather than being a broader ceasefire. Russian attacks elsewhere in Ukraine continued throughout the weekend.
Putin announced the pause as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to Moscow and Kyiv as part of Washington’s latest push to revive negotiations aimed at ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The temporary lull followed more than eight consecutive days of Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and the surrounding region, putting further strain on Ukraine’s air defenses.
During their meeting in Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelensky joked about the apparent effect of the envoys’ visit on the capital’s security.
“Today, you worked even better than the Patriot systems for our citizens here in the capital,” Zelensky told Witkoff and Kushner, urging them to visit more often.

articles.title: Russia Pounds Kyiv Hours After US Envoys Depart Ukrainian Capital
articles.body:
KYIV -- Russia hammered the Ukrainian capital with ballistic missiles, killing at least two people in a major attack hours after White House envoys left Kyiv amid a renewed push for peace negotiations.
The September 8 attack followed a lull in near daily attacks and underscored Russia's intent to press forward in its nearly 4 1/2-year war on Ukraine despite astronomical casualties.
Emergency workers pulled bodies from the rubble in one district of Kyiv while firefighters battled to put out fires from the attack, which also included jet-powered drones -- a relatively new weapon that Ukraine has struggled to defend against.
At least 10 people were wounded, emergency officials reported.
The Russian attack included dozens of ballistic and cruise missiles along with more than 160 drones overnight, Ukraine's military said.
Over the past week, Russia has hit Ukraine in near daily attacks. Ukraine’s ability to defend against the assaults has been severely constrained by a lack of missile interceptors, above all US-built Patriots.
The attack came hours after US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner departed Kyiv following meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and other officials. Prior to Kyiv, the pair visited Moscow for talks with President Vladimir Putin.
It was the first time the White House officials had traveled to Kyiv; by contrast, Witkoff has met with Putin eight times since the beginning of 2025.
US efforts to push peace negotiations have been dormant in recent months as Washington has prioritized the conflict with Iran, now in its sixth month.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha called on Kyiv's allies to "to act and increase pressure on the aggressor."
Russia's Defense Ministry said the attack targeted Ukrainian defense and military logistics facilities.
EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarina Mathernova said she spent the night in a shelter as "Kyiv was exploding and burning" during a Russian attack.
"What happened in Kyiv last night was hell," she wrote on X. "I would not wish it on anyone who lives in peace and falls asleep safely in their own bed."
After meeting Zelenskyy, Witkoff described discussions as constructive and said Washington had heard "new ideas" from Moscow. Kushner said the United States was working on a broader "peace package."
Zelenskyy, for his part, called his discussions with the Americans "very substantial" and said Ukraine was prepared to move toward trilateral talks involving Kyiv, Washington, and Moscow.
National-security advisers from Britain, France, and Germany also joined part of the Kyiv discussions.
The Kremlin has shown no indication it has softened its hard-line position on its war aims. In comments to reporters after the September 5 meetings with Putin, Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yury Ushakov said Russia would press forward to "eliminate" the "root causes" of the conflict.
"Root causes" is a phrase representing a grab bag of Russian grievances dating back to before the 2022 invasion, including the assertion that Zelenskyy is not a legitimate president and the Ukrainian government was oppressing native Russian speakers in Ukraine.

articles.title: UK commits £100m to bolster Ukraine’s air defences over winter
articles.body:
The UK has committed £100m to boost Ukraine’s air defences over winter by buying a package of US military equipment that will include a number of urgently needed Patriot missiles.
The air defence interceptors plus large-calibre artillery rounds and other drones will be supplied to Ukraine through a contribution to a Nato scheme to buy American weapons.
Ukraine is currently unable to prevent Russian ballistic missile attacks due to a shortage of Patriot interceptors, leading to attacks that have killed civilians and destroyed food and logistics warehouses over the summer.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he wants to obtain 300 Patriot missiles, costing about $3m (£2.6m) each, to help Kyiv protect its electricity, heating and water systems through the normally hard winter.
The UK did not say how many Patriots it would be able to buy, but the number is likely to be only a fraction of the number sought, though other western allies are also examining how they can help Kyiv defend itself.
The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, is due to co-chair his first meeting of the Ukraine defence contact group, made up of about 50 nations providing military equipment to Kyiv, with his German counterpart, Boris Pistorius, on Tuesday afternoon.
The virtual meeting, also due to be attended by Elbridge Colby, the US undersecretary for defence policy, will discuss how to further provide military aid to Ukraine as the war heads towards its fifth anniversary.
The UK recently agreed to declassify blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French-produced version of the Storm Shadow, which has already been used to hit targets in Russia.
Streeting said: “Both the prime minister and I heard loud and clear on our first visits to Kyiv the importance of supporting Ukraine through this winter, as Putin prepares to use winter as a weapon by continuing barbaric attacks against civilian and energy targets.
“We promised to mobilise allies and provide more support wherever we can. Today, we are delivering on that, strengthening Ukraine’s defences and, alongside 50 allies, converting commitment into capability.
“We will stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine until they win. Ukraine’s frontline is the frontline for freedom everywhere and our support will not waver.”
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to the US president, Donald Trump, about the war on Monday, with the two agreeing on the need to “continue working towards a ceasefire that prevented more loss of life”.
US envoys held talks in Kyiv on Sunday during an official visit to the country as part of an effort to end the conflict with Russia. While the talks were described as encouraging, no breakthrough was made. Zelenskyy said it appeared the war would continue into winter.

articles.title: Ukraine says TV channel building in capital Kyiv hit during Russian airstrike
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Ukraine said Tuesday that a daytime drone attack in the country’s capital Kyiv hit the building of a local TV channel, injuring at least five people.
In a statement on US social media company X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the drone strike partially destroyed the building of the My-Ukraina TV channel, part of the country’s United News telethon.
All necessary services are working, Zelenskyy said, adding that State Emergency Service personnel have already extinguished the fire that occurred at the site.
“As of now, five people have been reported injured. Unfortunately, that number may still rise,” Zelenskyy said, adding: “Not a single strike against Ukraine and Ukrainians – against life itself – can be left unpunished. Russia must be stopped, and this is possible only through joint efforts.”
The statement comes just hours after local authorities in Kyiv said that at least three people were killed and 19 others injured in overnight Russian drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram that the overnight strikes caused damage in the city's Darnytskyi, Holosiivskyi, Podilskyi, Shevchenkivskyi, and Solomianskyi districts, as well as in the Boryspil and Fastiv districts of the wider Kyiv region.
The strikes extended far beyond the capital, hitting key regions such as Dnipropetrovsk, Sumy, Odesa, and Kharkiv.
Ukraine's Air Force claimed that the country's air defenses shot down 142 out of 166 drones, as well as 33 missiles, launched by Russia overnight.
For its part, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed it launched overnight strikes on "Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, logistics and warehouse centers, and military installations" in Kyiv and the Kyiv region, among other targets in Ukraine.
Independent verification of the claims remains difficult due to the ongoing war.
The strikes mark a continuation of hostilities amid the Russia-Ukraine war. A three-day pause in strikes on Moscow and Kyiv until Monday evening had been declared while US envoys visited both countries' capitals over the weekend for peace talks.
Russia and Ukraine have increasingly targeted each other's logistics centers, as well as port and energy infrastructure, in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

articles.title: Russia pounds Kyiv in overnight attack, killing 3, injuring 16, as brief truce ends in missile fire
articles.body:
Russia pounds Kyiv in overnight attack, killing 3, injuring 19, as brief truce ends in missile fire
Smoke rising following a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, early on Sept. 8, 2026. (Eugene Kotenko / AFP via Getty Images)
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Key developments so far:
- Russia launched a large-scale drone and missile attack at Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight on Sept. 8, killing 3 people and injuring 19.
- The strike signals a definitive end to the aerial truce the Kremlin declared while Kyiv hosted U.S. officials for peace talks.
- The attack damaged residential buildings, a school, warehouses, and vehicles.
- Civilian infrastructure in Kyiv Oblast was also targeted, and one civilian injured.
- Air raid alerts sounded throughout the morning as Russian jet-powered drones continued to target the capital.
A mass Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv overnight on Sept. 8 killed at least three people, injured 19 others, and sparked a series of huge fires that filled the morning air across the city with smoke.
Residential buildings, a school, and warehouses were damaged in the attack, signaling a violent end to the brief respite for the capital during a diplomatic visit by U.S. envoys over the weekend.
"It's like The Hunger Games, it's just about survival," Dariia Kolisnyk, a resident of a building damaged by a missile in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, told the Kyiv Independent.
"You just go to bed, wondering whether you'll wake up or not. That's life in Kyiv."
The strike follows Russia and Ukraine's agreement to pause aerial attacks on each other's capitals for three days. While the precise expiration time of the truce was hazy, there is no doubt about its end.
Liudmyla Akhremenko, also a resident in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, said her home has been damaged for the second time in an attack in the area.
"The blast wave blew out the windows, and stones flew into the house. People’s furniture was damaged," Akhremenko told the Kyiv Independent.
According to Akhremenko, no shelter has yet been built nearby, so she was at home when the attack occurred.
"It was very scary," she said. "I was sleeping and woke up to the explosion. I saw that the windows had opened, the glass had shattered, and the flowers had fallen. Everything jumped up to the ceiling."
Explosions rang out in the capital at around 3:30 a.m. local time, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground. Another loud blast occurred about 10 minutes later.
At around 4:14 a.m. local time, Kyiv Independent journalist Yevgeniya Doluda reported a series of up to six explosions in rapid succession.
"There was a very strong bang," Kolisnyk said. "I opened my eyes and saw the window flying, and big flashes. I ran to the second room, where my child and my husband were sleeping and climbed through the broken door and windows."
"I got the child, thank God, sat him up, everything is fine. My husband was cut a little by the glass. But, thank God, everything is fine," she added.
The blasts followed warnings from Ukraine's Air Force that Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered strike drones were bound for Kyiv. Monitoring channels reported that at least 12 ballistic missiles have targeted the city in the span of about an hour.
The Air Force later reported that Russian forces launched 32 cruise missiles, 166 Shahed-type drones of which "more than half" were jet-powered, and an unspecified number of ballistic missiles. Two ballistic missiles, 31 cruise missiles, and 142 drones were intercepted, it said.
It added that missile and drone strikes were recorded at 29 locations.
At around 12:40 p.m. local time, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the death toll had risen to three.
As of 1 p.m. local time, 19 people had been injured in the attack in Kyiv, the Kyiv City Military Administration reported.
"The Russians tried to deliberately cause as much harm to life as possible — ballistics, cruise and anti-ship missiles, jet-powered 'shaheds,'" President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media.
Speaking to reporters later in the morning, Zelensky described the interception of almost all Russian cruise missiles as "a good result."
"Is it enough? No. We need (interceptor) missiles," he added. "We need a package of ballistic missiles from the Americans. They heard in detail what we need, when we need it."
"I count on meeting with President Trump to raise this topic. And, God willing, we will get a result."
At least two multistory residential buildings in the capital were damaged by drones, the Kyiv City Military Administration reported. Fires also broke out in warehouses, and garages and vehicles were reported damaged.

In an apparent sign of their resumption, air raid sirens sounded throughout the morning with the Air Force reporting several jet-powered drones in the airspace above Kyiv.
read also
The assault also targeted communities in the surrounding region, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Oblast Administration. Russia targeted the region from the evening of Sept. 7 into the morning of Sept. 8, targeting residential areas and civilian infrastructure.

Air raid alarms also sounded overnight in other regions of Ukraine, including Rivne Oblast in the northwest and other areas far from the front lines. The Air Force warned less than an hour earlier that Russia had likely launched cruise missiles from its Tu-95 and Tu-160 strategic bombers.
Moscow on Sept. 6 announced a three-day pause on attacks against Kyiv while U.S. Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the city for peace talks. The Kremlin declared the truce would "begin at midnight today," without specifying if that meant Sept. 5 or 6.

articles.title: Russia pounds Kiev, ending halt for US talks
articles.body:
Firefighters push out a fire following Russian missiles strikes in Kyiv early on September 8, 2026, amid the Russian invasion in Ukraine. (AFP Photo)
Russian missiles and drones pounded Kiev on Sept. 8, killing two people and sending smoke billowing above the Ukrainian capital, ending Moscow’s temporary halt to strikes on the city.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered the pause in attacks as U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the Russian and Ukrainian capitals at the weekend.
“The moment the U.S. president’s peace envoys left, Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kiev, damaging residential areas and killing at least two people,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said on social media.
“His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy.”
Witkoff and Kushner’s trips provided no immediate breakthrough in ending the four-and-a-half-year war, but represented Washington’s reengagement with trying to broker a deal between the two sides, which had been on hold for months.
Kiev Mayor Vitali Klitschko said people were trapped in a residential building after the strikes.
Russia’s army said it had a carried out a “massive strike” on military-industrial sites, logistics hubs and storage centers in Kiev and its suburbs.
Civilian deaths in Ukraine are running at their highest rate since the first months of Russia’s invasion, according to statistics verified by the United Nations.
In the Moscow-annexed Crimean peninsula, Russian-installed officials said a Ukrainian attack killed two people.
The strikes came hours after Witkoff touted “substantive progress” in the discussions with Ukraine and Russia, raising the prospect of reviving three-way peace talks to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.
“President Trump is working hard to stop the killing and work towards a lasting and durable peace,” he said on X.
Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Sept. 5, before holding separate talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in their first official trip to Kiev.
The Kremlin announced on Sept. 7 that it did not rule out three-way talks, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov telling reporters “it is too early to say anything about the venue or the exact dates at this stage.”
Zelensky told U.S. news outlet Axios that the U.S. was pushing to deescalate the conflict ahead of the long winter.
Russia has struck Ukraine’s energy grid each winter since invading in February 2022, cutting power and heating to millions in temperatures as low as -20 degrees Celsius.
Zelensky has said the weekend talks included U.S. proposals around energy facilities, grain shipments and oil and gas exports, but declined to give further details.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on Sept. 5 appeared to rule out a Turkish proposal for a truce on strikes in the Black Sea, saying it was “unrealistic” and “impossible to monitor.”
The two sides appear no close to agreeing on how the war should end.
Moscow is demanding Ukraine cede territory in its eastern Donetsk region that it still controls and renounce Western military support.
Kiev has said such terms amount to capitulation and would only allow Russia to prepare a fresh attack in its bid to install a Moscow-friendly puppet government.

articles.title: U.S. and Russian warplanes to appear together at Egypt’s airshow
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force is sending F-16s, F-15Es, A-10s and C-130s to Egypt's El Alamein International Airshow, opening September 8 alongside more than 80 countries.
- Russia is separately showcasing its Su-57E stealth fighter at the same airshow, putting American and Russian military aircraft on display together.
American and Russian military aircraft will appear at the same airshow this week, as the U.S. Air Force sends fighters and cargo planes to Egypt’s El Alamein International Airshow alongside a Russian delegation set to showcase its Su-57E stealth fighter.
The 2026 Egypt International Airshow officially opens September 8 at El Alamein International Airport, drawing participants from more than 80 countries and more than 50 aircraft on display, according to a statement from U.S. Central Command. The event marks its second iteration and is intended to highlight Egypt’s aerospace capabilities while reinforcing the decades-long U.S.-Egypt defense relationship.
The U.S. Air Force and the Texas Air National Guard are sending personnel and aircraft to the show, including C-130J Super Hercules and C-130H Hercules cargo planes, A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft, F-16 Fighting Falcon fighters, and F-15E Strike Eagle strike fighters. The U.S. delegation is also opening a pavilion featuring more than 25 American aerospace and defense companies.
“The United States is proud to participate in the El Alamein International Air Show 2026 and to open the U.S. Pavilion, featuring more than 25 American companies from among the world’s leading aerospace and defense innovators,” said Eric Gaudiosi, Charge d’Affaires ad interim at the U.S. Embassy in Cairo. “Our strong presence reflects the depth of the U.S.-Egypt partnership and our longstanding cooperation across the aviation, aerospace, defense, space, and commercial sectors. We look forward to building new partnerships and expanding opportunities that benefit both our countries.”
Russia is also attending the show with its own aircraft. Russia’s state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport, has said it will fly its Su-57E stealth fighter in a demonstration and display it on the ground, alongside the public debut of two new weapons built for the jet, according to Russian state media reports covered separately by The Defence Blog. Rosoboronexport CEO Alexander Mikheev has said the company has signed new Su-57E export contracts ahead of the show, though he has not named the buying countries or disclosed contract values, and Russia’s claims about the jet’s proven combat record have not matched independently documented losses of the aircraft during its war in Ukraine.
Egypt has maintained defense ties with both Washington and Moscow for decades, operating American-made F-16s alongside Russian-made air defense systems and other Soviet-legacy equipment, a balancing act reflected in this week’s airshow drawing military hardware from both countries onto the same tarmac. The U.S.-Egypt defense relationship dates back to the 1978 Camp David Accords, and Egypt remains one of the largest recipients of U.S. military aid in the world.

articles.title: Iran vows to strike the Gulf's energy infrastructure
articles.body:
Various states have warned of major consequences if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Majed Al-Ansari, remarked to US media that opening the Strait of Hormuz is a priority, as the world faces an "industrial catastrophe"
Average of 10 commodity ships transited Hormuz per day over the past 10 days, marking the lowest level since May following US and Iranian strikes on tankers, Kpler data shows
Israeli attacks have continued on south Lebanon, Gaza, occupied West Bank, and south Syria despite any agreements or alleged ceasefires
Saudi-led coalition in Yemen says recent Houthi attacks on civilian and economic sites in Saudi Arabia have injured 73 people, including women and children
Britain's foreign minister Ed Miliband said on Tuesday that Britain is sanctioning Hezbollah-run financial institution Al-Qard Al-Hassan, as he announced a trade ban on goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Lebanon's central bank last year banned banks and brokerages from dealing with Al-Qard Al-Hassan, which describes itself as a charitable organisation that provides loans to people according to Islamic principles that forbid interest.
Houthi media in Yemen reported a series of Saudi strikes on Tuesday after a wave of attacks by the rebels injured dozens in southern Saudi Arabia.
"The Saudi aggression launches a series of raids on Al-Waziyah district" in Taiz province, where fighting has raged for days, Almasirah television said, after also reporting four Saudi strikes in Marib province.
Iran says 'significant progress' in talks with Oman
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tuesday there had been "significant progress" in talks with Oman over the administration of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
According to an Iranian foreign ministry statement, Araghchi "explained the latest status of Iran-Oman talks on the Strait of Hormuz, reporting significant progress" during a call with his Japanese counterpart.
Iran and Oman, both coastal states on the strait, have for weeks been discussing the future of navigation through the waterway, with Tehran saying progress had been made to agree a temporary shipping route.
Iranian forces have restricted traffic through Hormuz, a vital energy conduit, since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on 28 February.
The US has imposed a counter naval blockade on Iranian ports.
President Donald Trump said in recent days that American forces have helped facilitate the passage of vessels through the strait, "averaging 30 ships a night".
Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said Sunday that the US tries each night to help five or six ships through, "and usually these ships get hit".
Tehran has required vessels to seek permission to transit, insisting there will be no return to the pre-war system of unrestricted navigation.
It has also sought to impose service fees on ships using the strait—a move strongly opposed by Washington and regional countries.
Iranian officials recently said a deal between Oman and Iran could be signed "in the coming days".
They have however insisted the strait will not reopen until the United States meets Iranian demands, including removing oil sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets abroad and lifting the naval blockade on Iranian ports.
An Israeli court on Tuesday rejected a bid from rights groups to halt development of a settlement in the occupied West Bank that would break the territorial contiguity of a future Palestinian state.
The Jerusalem District Court said in a ruling it had dismissed the motion, which aimed to stall the publication of tenders for the settlement east of Jerusalem.
Last month, Israel's construction and housing ministry opened a tender for construction of more than 1,200 housing units, leading NGOs to file motions against it.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun condemned what he described as "terrorist attacks that targeted several Saudi cities today, (...) which affected civilian and economic figures, and led to the injury of a number of civilians, including women and children."
"We in Lebanon are following with great concern this dangerous escalation that targets the security and stability of the sister Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and we strongly condemn this aggressive act, which constitutes a clear violation of the sovereignty of a sister country and a direct threat to the safety of its citizens and those residing on its lands," he said.
"Lebanon's full solidarity, as president and people, with the leadership and people of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the face of this sinful attack," Aoun affirmed, further stressing that "the Kingdom's security is an integral part of the security of Lebanon and the entire Arab region, and that any targeting of its sovereignty requires unified Arab and international condemnation."
CNN: Washington mulls reducing military presence in region
CNN, citing six sources, reported that quiet discussions recently took place within the US military and intelligence circles regarding reducing the number of personnel and facilities usually deployed in the Middle East, if the administration of President Donald Trump succeeds in ending the conflict with Iran.
According to the network, the implementation of these reductions will represent a new shift in how the US national security agencies deal with the region, after the United States expanded, in the wake of the attacks of 11 September 2001, its network of permanent military and intelligence facilities to carry out operations and wars in a number of countries in the region.
CNN indicated that the recent confrontation with Iran revealed major weaknesses in the US infrastructure in the region, after several facilities became targets of repeated Iranian attacks, in a war that resulted in the death of 18 US soldiers.
UK publishes legislation for tougher sanctions on Iran
Britain on Tuesday published legislation to introduce tougher sanctions on Iran, expanding trade restrictions and powers to target ships as part of what it described as wider effort to curb Tehran's nuclear programme and other hostile activities.
The government said the measures would restrict Iran's access to the British financial system, expand trade bans to additional goods, technology and services, and prohibit Iranian aircraft from landing in Britain unless exemptions apply.
Surviving the US war, sanctions and inflation in Iran
Iran's inflation crisis is squeezing families as sanctions, the US war, and a currency collapse drive up food, healthcare, fuel, and living costs, writes Ariya Farahmand.
Nicaragua Tuesday accused Germany of "multiple violations of international law" at the United Nations top court, as it pressed its case that Berlin is complicit in the Israeli genocide of Gaza.
The central American country has dragged Germany to the International Court of Justice in The Hague, accusing Berlin of breaching the 1948 UN Genocide Convention with its support, notably arms shipments, for Israel.
"Nicaragua invokes Germany's responsibility in connection to multiple violations of international law, particularly in respect of the odious scourge of genocide and international humanitarian law," ambassador Carlos Jose Arguello Gomez told the court.
Gomez said Nicaragua's claims "involve the most serious breaches of obligations arising under... general international law."
Germany is now seeking to have it thrown out completely, arguing that judges do not have jurisdiction and that Nicaragua's case does not hold water.
On Monday, the first of four days of hearings, Germany's representative Julia Monar argued Germany's "unwavering support for the existence and security of the State of Israel" but also said it was one of the world's largest bilateral donors to the Palestinian Territories.
"All German exports of military technology and equipment to Israel -- as to any country -- are subject to strict licensing requirements which exceed international requirements," she said.
It takes on average six months for the court to hand down a ruling in such cases.
The court could either side with Germany and throw out the case completely or rule against Berlin, meaning the case would then be considered "on the merits" in more detail.
Qatar PM, Chinese FM discuss Hormuz navigation in Beijing
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani and China’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Wang Yi have discussed regional developments, including the freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, in a meeting in Beijing, according to the foreign ministry’s statement on X.
Sheikh Mohammed affirmed Qatar’s support for all diplomatic efforts aimed at ensuring maritime navigation and "paving the way for a comprehensive agreement".
Asia stocks fall as yen surges, Iran warns US of retaliation
A surge in the yen and mixed economic data sent Asian stocks lower on Tuesday, while fresh Iranian threats in the Gulf drove commodity prices and Treasury bond yields higher.
The yen jumped as much as 1% to 152.89, its strongest level since 18 February, as investors unwound an estimated $2.35 trillion in yen-funded carry trades.
"The yen has rallied to its strongest level since February, driven by a sharp unwinding of short-yen and carry-trade positions as investors price in faster Bank of Japan tightening," said Joel Kruger, market strategist at LMAX Group in London.
"Speculation over capital repatriation by Japanese investors and the authorities' demonstrated willingness to support the currency through intervention have added momentum to the move."
Japan's Nikkei 225 share index fluctuated between gains and losses before lurching down 1.7%, as S&P 500 e-mini futures slid 0.3% after a holiday in the US on Monday.
MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was 0.5% lower, with regional declines led by a 1% fall in Australian shares after a measure of local consumer sentiment fell sharply in September.
Oil prices rose for a third day in Asia, with Brent crude futures climbing 1.4% to $98.34 a barrel, after Iran threatened to retaliate on Tuesday against the US with "economic warfare" and said it had fired an advanced missile at US warships.
"While US Labor Day made for a somewhat quieter start to the week for trading volumes, the weekend’s tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran continued to put upward pressure on oil prices, acting as a drag on risk sentiment more broadly," Westpac analysts said.
Oil prices are rising amid tensions in the region with Brent crude trading today at around $98, an increase of nearly 2%, and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude is trading at around $94.
Oil prices are rising as tensions brew in the region. [Getty]
Netanyahu under fire over report UAE warned of Oct 7 attack
Israeli opposition leaders on Tuesday called Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu unfit to serve after a report that the United Arab Emirates had warned him before the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack.
Haaretz newspaper, in a report excerpted from a forthcoming book by its reporters, said UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan spoke to Netanyahu a week and a half before the attack and told him that Hamas was planning a major operation.
Netanyahu's office called the report by the Israeli newspaper "an absolute lie" and denied he spoke to the Emirati leader at that time.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former military commander who has emerged as Netanyahu's top rival in upcoming 27 October elections, accused the long-serving prime minister of evading responsibility for security lapses and resorting to "pathetic" excuses, such as saying he was not woken up soon enough on the morning of the attack.
"Netanyahu received dozens of warnings for October 7 and ignored them all. He is unfit," Eisenkot wrote on X.
Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister also running in elections, said Netanyahu "bears personal and direct responsibility" for the deaths on October 7, the deadliest attack in Israeli history.
"Netanyahu cannot continue to serve in his position for even one more minute," Bennett said.
Haaretz said that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, later killed by Israel, had warned a former Palestinian official that the militants were preparing "a terrifying operation" which he described as an "earthquake".
The former Palestinian official relayed the message to an Emirati advisor, who passed it on to the Emirati leader who then called Netanyahu, according to the newspaper.
The UAE 'normalised' ties with Israel in 2020 as part of the US-brokered Abraham Accords under President Donald Trump's first administration.
Netanyahu sees close ties with the UAE as a key achievement.
US Ambassdor Hucakbee warns UK off Israeli settlement ban
American will react to the UK's expected announcement of a ban on trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee says.
Huckabee told BBC News, "I think without a doubt there will be" a reaction, including at the level of individual states.
This could have a "huge economic impact on British businesses," he says, explaining some could be banned from doing business in certain states.
Britain will announce a trade ban on goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank later on Tuesday, confirmed a senior minister, as part of the UK's efforts to support a two-state solution.
Six weeks into his new job, foreign minister Ed Miliband flagged last week that he was looking at resetting Britain's policy on Israel, and he is due to make a statement on Israel and trading restrictions in the House of Commons.
Britain's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, also in office since July, spoke to US President Donald Trump on Monday to stress the "the importance of the two-state solution", in what is seen as a reference to the sanctions.
Miliband said last week that Israel's E1 settlement project in the occupied West Bank would cut across land which the Palestinians seek for a state, putting at risk the two-state solution.
Asked about how the trade ban would operate, pensions minister Pat McFadden did not give details.
"The foreign secretary will make a statement to Parliament later today," McFadden told Times Radio. "The reason that danger has become more urgent is because of expanded settlement activity in recent weeks and months."
UN bodies and most governments, including Britain, consider Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank illegal under international law.
Saudi Arabia condemns Houthi attacks on its territory
Saudi Arabia on Tuesday condemned Houthi attacks on its territory that wounded 73 people, saying it will "take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty".
The foreign ministry, in a statement carried by the official Saudi Press Agency, called for an "immediate halt to all forms of escalation practised by this militia" as well as Houthi attacks on shipping.
Hormuz traffic slows after Iran threatens retaliation
Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz slowed at the start of this week, after Iran threatened on Monday to retaliate for any new US attacks.
The number of commodity vessels sailing through the Strait of Hormuz totalled seven on Monday, compared with eight on the previous day, Kpler data showed on Tuesday.
Iran had warned that energy infrastructure across the Gulf, including US oil and gas interests, was vulnerable.
Goldman Sachs also raised its Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude oil price forecasts for December 2026 and 2027, as it expects shipping disruptions in the Middle East to persist into next year.
Traffic increased through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, however, another major waterway for commodity vessels.
A total of 29 commodity vessels passed through Bab al-Mandeb on Monday, up from 17 on the previous day, Kpler data showed.
Some vessels may be sailing through the two straits with their transponders off, which is not considered in the counts.
Iran-backed Houthis attack Saudi cities, 73 wounded
Iran-backed Houthi militia attacked several cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding 73 people, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Tuesday, a further sign that the conflict risks spreading into a wider regional war as diplomatic progress stalls.
Iran threatened the United States with "economic warfare" on Tuesday and said it had fired an advanced missile at US warships, underscoring the risks of further escalation in the war only days after both sides traded blows again.
The six-month-old war has been marked by a cycle of pauses followed by periodic flare-ups, with the US last reporting attacks on Iranian targets on Saturday, when US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers. Iranian state media on Sunday reported that Iran fired the Qassem Basir missile in its attacks on several US vessels.
And despite U.S. attempts to open up the Strait of Hormuz, Iran has continued to disrupt shipping through the critical artery for global oil and gas supplies, with commodity vessel traffic slowing again this week.
The Islamic Republic has vowed to announce a new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days, along with maps of a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, though it was unclear when details would emerge.

Oil prices are rising amid tensions in the region with Brent crude trading today at around $98, an increase of nearly 2%, and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude is trading at around $94.
Oil prices are rising as tensions brew in the region. [Getty]
Netanyahu under fire over report UAE warned of Oct 7 attack
Israeli opposition leaders on Tuesday called Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu unfit to serve after a report that the United Arab Emirates had warned him before the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack.
Haaretz newspaper, in a report excerpted from a forthcoming book by its reporters, said UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan spoke to Netanyahu a week and a half before the attack and told him that Hamas was planning a major operation.
Netanyahu's office called the report by the Israeli newspaper "an absolute lie" and denied he spoke to the Emirati leader at that time.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former military commander who has emerged as Netanyahu's top rival in upcoming 27 October elections, accused the long-serving prime minister of evading responsibility for security lapses and resorting to "pathetic" excuses, such as saying he was not woken up soon enough on the morning of the attack.
"Netanyahu received dozens of warnings for October 7 and ignored them all. He is unfit," Eisenkot wrote on X.
Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister also running in elections, said Netanyahu "bears personal and direct responsibility" for the deaths on October 7, the deadliest attack in Israeli history.
"Netanyahu cannot continue to serve in his position for even one more minute," Bennett said.
Haaretz said that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, later killed by Israel, had warned a former Palestinian official that the militants were preparing "a terrifying operation" which he described as an "earthquake".
The former Palestinian official relayed the message to an Emirati advisor, who passed it on to the Emirati leader who then called Netanyahu, according to the newspaper.
The UAE 'normalised' ties with Israel in 2020 as part of the US-brokered Abraham Accords under President Donald Trump's first administration.
Netanyahu sees close ties with the UAE as a key achievement.
US Ambassdor Hucakbee warns UK off Israeli settlement ban
American will react to the UK's expected announcement of a ban on trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee says.
Huckabee told BBC News, "I think without a doubt there will be" a reaction, including at the level of individual states.
This could have a "huge economic impact on British businesses," he says, explaining some could be banned from doing business in certain states.
Britain will announce a trade ban on goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank later on Tuesday, confirmed a senior minister, as part of the UK's efforts to support a two-state solution.
Six weeks into his new job, foreign minister Ed Miliband flagged last week that he was looking at resetting Britain's policy on Israel, and he is due to make a statement on Israel and trading restrictions in the House of Commons.
Britain's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, also in office since July, spoke to US President Donald Trump on Monday to stress the "the importance of the two-state solution", in what is seen as a reference to the sanctions.
Miliband said last week that Israel's E1 settlement project in the occupied West Bank would cut across land which the Palestinians seek for a state, putting at risk the two-state solution.
Asked about how the trade ban would operate, pensions minister Pat McFadden did not give details.
"The foreign secretary will make a statement to Parliament later today," McFadden told Times Radio. "The reason that danger has become more urgent is because of expanded settlement activity in recent weeks and months."
UN bodies and most governments, including Britain, consider Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank illegal under international law.
Saudi Arabia condemns Houthi attacks on its territory
Saudi Arabia on Tuesday condemned Houthi attacks on its territory that wounded 73 people, saying it will "take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty".
The foreign ministry, in a statement carried by the official Saudi Press Agency, called for an "immediate halt to all forms of escalation practised by this militia" as well as Houthi attacks on shipping.
Hormuz traffic slows after Iran threatens retaliation
Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz slowed at the start of this week, after Iran threatened on Monday to retaliate for any new US attacks.
The number of commodity vessels sailing through the Strait of Hormuz totalled seven on Monday, compared with eight on the previous day, Kpler data showed on Tuesday.
Iran had warned that energy infrastructure across the Gulf, including US oil and gas interests, was vulnerable.
Goldman Sachs also raised its Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude oil price forecasts for December 2026 and 2027, as it expects shipping disruptions in the Middle East to persist into next year.
Traffic increased through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, however, another major waterway for commodity vessels.
A total of 29 commodity vessels passed through Bab al-Mandeb on Monday, up from 17 on the previous day, Kpler data showed.
Some vessels may be sailing through the two straits with their transponders off, which is not considered in the counts.
Iran-backed Houthis attack Saudi cities, 73 wounded
Iran-backed Houthi militia attacked several cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding 73 people, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Tuesday, a further sign that the conflict risks spreading into a wider regional war as diplomatic progress stalls.
Iran threatened the United States with "economic warfare" on Tuesday and said it had fired an advanced missile at US warships, underscoring the risks of further escalation in the war only days after both sides traded blows again.
The six-month-old war has been marked by a cycle of pauses followed by periodic flare-ups, with the US last reporting attacks on Iranian targets on Saturday, when US forces struck three Iranian oil tankers. Iranian state media on Sunday reported that Iran fired the Qassem Basir missile in its attacks on several US vessels.
And despite U.S. attempts to open up the Strait of Hormuz, Iran has continued to disrupt shipping through the critical artery for global oil and gas supplies, with commodity vessel traffic slowing again this week.
The Islamic Republic has vowed to announce a new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days, along with maps of a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, though it was unclear when details would emerge.

articles.title: 'As much harm as possible' — 5 killed, 63 injured as Russia resumes mass attacks across Ukraine
articles.body:
'As much harm as possible' — 5 killed, 63 injured as Russia resumes mass attacks across Ukraine
At least five people were killed and 63 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Sept. 8.
The mass attacks marked the end of a brief pause in strikes that was in place during a weekend visit by U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv. The talks failed to produce a major breakthrough, with President Volodymyr Zelensky saying afterward that he expected the war to continue into the winter.
The overnight attack underscored that reports, as Russia launched a large-scale missile and drone attack across Ukraine, with Kyiv and Odesa Oblast among the main targets, according to Ukraine's Air Force.
"It was a difficult attack, which the Russians deliberately tried to calculate to cause as much harm to life as possible: ballistic missiles, cruise and anti-ship missiles, jet-powered Shaheds," Zelensky said.
As of 8:30 a.m., with the attack still ongoing, air defenses had downed or suppressed two ballistic missiles, 31 cruise missiles, and 142 drones. Strikes were recorded at 29 locations, while debris from intercepted drones and missiles fell at nine additional sites, the Air Force said.
"Despite very good results against cruise missiles, ballistic missiles remain particularly difficult, and every day we make clear to our partners our need for interceptors," Zelensky added.
In Kyiv, at least three people were killed and 19 others were injured in a mass Russian missile and drone attack, city authorities said. Residential buildings, a school, and warehouses were damaged, while several large fires broke out across the capital.
As the attack continued, at nearly 12:00 p.m., Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said drone debris had fallen on a four-story office building in Solomianskyi district, causing a fire and structural damage. People were being evacuated from the upper floors, with preliminary reports indicating that there were casualties.
The assault also targeted communities in the surrounding region, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Oblast Administration. One person was injured in a strike in the town of Bila Tserkva, Tkachenko added.
In Donetsk Oblast, two people were killed and 10 others were injured by Russian attacks, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
Two people were killed in Kramatorsk, where six others were wounded. The security situation in the city has deteriorated as Russian forces continue their gradual advance toward it. Three people were also injured in Sloviansk and one in Raihorodok.
One person was killed and 13 others were injured by Russian attacks in Kherson Oblast, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, 12 people were injured in Russian attacks, Governor Ivan Fedorov said.
In Kharkiv Oblast, three people, including a 17-year-old boy, were injured by Russian attacks, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. The attacks continued into the morning, with Syniehubov reporting at 9:41 a.m. that a Russian drone had preliminarily struck central Kharkiv.
Three men aged 58, 54, and 48 were injured in a Russian attack on a market in the suburbs of Odesa, with the 58-year-old hospitalized in moderate condition, Governor Oleh Kiper said.
In Sumy Oblast, a 65-year-old man was injured in a Russian drone strike, local authorities said.
On the morning of Sept. 8, Russian drones struck a Kyiv-Sumy passenger train twice, but no one was injured after the train was stopped during an air raid alert and all 90 passengers and crew members were evacuated, Governor Oleh Hryhorov said.
In Chernihiv Oblast, a 40-year-old woman was injured in a Russian drone attack on the village of Pryluky, Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
One person was injured by Russian attacks in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, local authorities said.

articles.body:
Moscow says it will have a 'harsh and painful' response to Hungarian move to expel 10 diplomats
We are getting a bit more on that Russian response to Hungary, and it’s clear that Moscow is not happy.
The foreign ministry said it would proceed with a “harsh and painful” response, AFP reported.
“The response to the Russophobic lobby in Budapest will be harsh and painful,” foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told the TASS state news agency.
Ukraine has been asking western allies for air defence equipment amid fears Russia will dramatically intensify its missile attacks this winter. My colleagues Jamie Grierson and Dan Sabbaghhave written a story about the UK committing to £100m to boost Ukraine’s air defences ahead of the anticipated attacks. We already mentioned the pledge in this post, but their story contains more detail. Here is an extract:
The air defence interceptors plus large-calibre artillery rounds and other drones will be supplied to Ukraine through a contribution to a Nato scheme to buy American weapons.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he wants to obtain 300 Patriot missiles, costing about $3m (£2.6m) each, to help Kyiv protect its electricity, heating and water systems through the normally hard winter.
The UK did not say how many Patriots it would be able to buy, but the number is likely to be only a fraction of the number sought, though other western allies are also examining how they can help Kyiv defend itself.
40-year-old Russian man questioned over Romanian sabotage allegations
A 40-year-old Russian man suspected of being involved in the operation is being questioned by Romanian prosecutors on Tuesday, a statement from Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism said.
Authorities are seeking court approval to detain him for 30 days pending inquiries into his encrypted communications, which reportedly included photos of several Romanian and multinational military bases.
Romanian intelligence service says it prevented Russian sabotage operation targeting defence, critical infrastructure
Romanian intelligence service said it “prevented the commission of a sabotage on national territory,” involving a Russian citizen in Romania and a number of defence and critical infrastructure targets.
In a statement, the SRI service said that the Russian man, who was being monitored as part of an extensive investigation, attempted to take photo and video documentation of “some communications centres and national military bases used by Nato allies,” as well as other defence institutions and critical infrastructure.
“The data obtained indicate a similar action pattern to that used on the territory of European states by networks of saboteurs coordinated by entities from the Russian Federation, including in the cases thwarted in Romania in 2024 and 2025: the Russian citizen was instructed by an intermediary to make photo-video materials with targets of strategic military interest, including a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft during their presence on the national territory.”
It added that “the specific actions taken by the SRI, as well as the measures taken with the Romanian authorities and external partners, led to the prevention of an act of sabotage on national territory.”
The service did not offer more detail on whether it involved any arrests.
Dutch foreign minister calls for 'accountability, reconciliation, education' after Serbia's 'hero' funeral for Mladić
Dutch foreign minister Tom Berendsen also joined in calls for “accountability, reconciliation and education about the past” as he criticised Serbia for holding a “hero” funeral for Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić (12:48).
“Ratko Mladić was convicted of war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. The honour bestowed upon him in Belgrade by the state is incompatible with European values and deeply hurtful to victims and their families.
The Netherlands supports voices in Serbia and across the region calling for accountability, reconciliation and education about the past.”
German police detain suspect after sabotage attacks on power grid
Elsewhere, we are getting a line from Germany that German police have detained a man suspected of carrying out a series of sabotage attacks on the country’s electricity grid, as reported by local media and Reuters.
The suspect, identified as Daniel V. by German media, was detained in Weisweiler about 50 kilometres (30 miles) west of Cologne, where he allegedly carried out one of his attempted attacks, Reuters said.
German police have been searching for the 48-year-old since they obtained letters claiming responsibility for a series of sabotage attacks on the power grid, in which the suspect cited opposition to fossil fuels as a motive.
German news agency DPA said that the suspect’s “motive was reportedly climate-related, with the letters criticising electricity production from fossil fuels.”
EU backs Hungary's decision to expel 10 Russian diplomats
Separately, the commission was also asked about Hungary’s decision to expel 10 Russian diplomats this morning.
The commission’s foreign affairs spokesperson Christian Wigand said:
“We take note of Hungary’s legitimate decision.
This is an expected reaction [given] Russia’s persistent campaign in using hybrid attacks against the EU and its member states.
The European Union expresses its full solidarity with Hungary and reaffirms its support for the diplomatic and consular activities of all member states conducted in accordance with international law.
The European Union will continue to closely coordinate with Hungary and other member states, and remains committed to protecting the interests and the rights of EU citizens.”
Bosnia withdraws diplomatic staff from Serbia in protest at Mladić's 'hero' funeral
It’s worth noting that Bosnia and Herzegovina withdrew all staff from its Belgrade embassy yesterday, and transferred consular services to its embassies in Zagreb and Podgorica in protest against Mladić’s ‘hero’ funeral in Belgrade.
The ministry saidthe move intended to “reduce communication with Serbia to the lowest possible level,” while intensifying its dialogue about the situation with the EU, US, and the UK.
It’s also probably safe to say that the Bosnian foreign ministry was not impressed with the commission’s bland holding position yesterday.
Responding to questions from reporters yesterday, the EU’s lead spokesperson Paula Pinho insisted that “there is no place for glorification of war criminals,” but did not really engage with repeated questions about the apparent state and military honours involved.
In a late afternoon post directed at Pinho, the ministry said: “are you even aware of what you are saying?”
It continued:
“Five ministers from the Serbian Government were seated in the front row at the funeral, a convicted war criminal was given military honours, and his body was flown in on a Serbian Government aircraft.
What are you afraid of? Why are you unwilling to call this what it is?
Your position on the funeral of a convicted war criminal is a disgrace to the entire European Union!”
Difficult not to see a link between their furious reaction and this morning’s hasty statement from von der Leyen and Pinho’s notably different tone at today’s midday briefing.
EU 'looking into' its response to Serbia's 'hero' funeral for Mladić
Not surprisingly, the issue of the EU’s muddled response to yesterday’s “hero” funeral for Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić comes up again during today’s midday briefing held by the European Commission.
A commission spokesperson said the commission was “looking into” any potential consequences for Serbia.
She also repeated commission president von der Leyen’s criticism from this morning (9:41), saying the images from the funeral were “shocking” and “speak for themselves.”
“They demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe’s recent history and contradict the values underpinning Serbia’s path towards the European Union,” Paula Pinho said.
She declined to say if von der Leyen would visit Belgrade on her annual trip to western Balkans, stressing the programme is still being worked on.

The foreign ministry said it would proceed with a “harsh and painful” response, AFP reported.
“The response to the Russophobic lobby in Budapest will be harsh and painful,” foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told the TASS state news agency.
Russia to respond to Hungary's decision to expel 10 Russian diplomats

articles.title: Zelensky gives cautious backing to Trump envoys' 'good' ideas to end Russia's war
articles.body:
Zelensky gives cautious backing to Trump envoys' 'good' ideas to end Russia's war
U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, brought Kyiv some "pretty good, decent" ideas on how to end Russia's war against Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters on Sept. 8.
Zelensky said it remains unclear whether the proposals can actually work.
"We need to understand whether we can implement them and make them effective," the Ukrainian president said. "I don't know yet if it will work out."
His comments came days after Witkoff and Kushner traveled to Moscow and Kyiv with revised peace proposals in an apparent attempt to restart negotiations that have been deadlocked for months.
Zelensky stopped short of disclosing the details of the U.S. proposals but pointed to two issues that could play an important role in any potential agreement: grain and energy.
"Grain and energy are sensitive issues for Ukraine and Russia," he said.
Grain, energy
One new proposal discussed during the talks involved a potential truce in the air, either focused on energy infrastructure or halting aerial strikes altogether, one person familiar with the negotiations previously told the Kyiv Independent.
Russia has not agreed to the proposal so far.
Both Ukraine and Russia have repeatedly targeted each other's energy infrastructure throughout the war. While Ukraine has targeted Russia's energy exports to cut off a key source of funding for the war, Moscow has focused on destroying Ukrainian power plants and substations in an effort to trigger blackouts across the country.
The issue has become particularly urgent for Kyiv ahead of another winter, when Ukrainian officials expect Russia to intensify attacks on the country's energy grid.
Last winter, Kyiv faced a major Russian campaign against its energy infrastructure, causing mass blackouts amid freezing temperatures.
Grain has also emerged as another sensitive issue.
Russia has intensified attacks on shipping corridors in the Black Sea, including deadly strikes on civilian grain ships. The campaign has contributed to declining exports, rising costs, and a shrinking number of vessels willing to dock at Ukrainian ports.
Zelensky said the consequences extend far beyond Ukraine and Russia.
"These are pressing issues for the entire world," he said. "And these are pressing issues for India today, for the Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Asia, and many other countries. We are ready to find a compromise here."
read also
Meeting with Trump
Zelensky said he hopes to meet Trump around Sept. 20 and plans to raise Ukraine's need for additional anti-ballistic missiles.
"We need a package of anti-ballistic missiles from the U.S. They heard in detail what we need," Zelensky said. "I count on meeting with President Trump to raise this topic."
Ukraine faces a shortage of missiles capable of intercepting Russian ballistic missiles, which Moscow has increasingly used against Ukrainian cities.
Zelensky did not disclose the details of the proposed support package.
"I cannot disclose all the details here," he said. "We have agreed with the American side that we will prepare everything and then communicate with the Europeans."
Moscow's demands remain
Despite the renewed U.S. push, the central obstacles to a peace deal remain unchanged.
The negotiations have been effectively deadlocked since earlier this year as Moscow continues to reject a ceasefire along the current front lines and demands that Ukraine cede Donbas — the strategically important, partially occupied region in eastern Ukraine — and abandon its NATO membership aspirations.
The Kremlin has not signaled that it is prepared to compromise on its territorial demands.
At the same time, Ukrainian officials warn that Russia is preparing to escalate attacks on Ukrainian cities and the country's energy infrastructure over the winter.
"Putin still hopes to break us this winter and isn't willing to agree to anything," one Ukrainian official previously told the Kyiv Independent.

articles.title: Ukraine has 67 companies working to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones en masse, Zelenskyy says. Only three to five have real results
articles.body:
Ukraine now has 67 companies working to shoot down Russia's jet-powered drones en masse, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. He gave the number at a Kyiv press conference alongside US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Ukrinform reported.
Most of those firms are still chasing the problem, and only a few have working systems. The race matters because Russia's jet-powered Geran drones fly too fast for the mobile gun teams that once downed the slower models. Russia has sharply expanded the jets' use over the summer, launching them by day as well as by night and driving air-raid alerts over Kyiv almost hourly.
Prototypes outnumber proven interceptors
"Today, we have about 60 companies in Ukraine already working on intercepting jet-powered drones, and doing so on a mass scale. To be precise, there are 67," Zelenskyy said.
He added that three to five have shown real results, and the next step is mass production.
Zelenskyy calls it all "Plan B"
Zelenskyy framed the entire defensive build-up as a fallback.
"All this defense is 'Plan B,' though right now it is very relevant. 'Plan A' is to accelerate diplomatic possibilities as much as possible, to reduce escalation from Russia," he said.
He spoke as the US envoys pressed a peace push in Kyiv, with no breakthrough announced.
He also called anti-ballistic defense Ukraine's weak point, saying he would raise it in upcoming meetings in Norway and Canada, and that the US plans to increase production of Patriot interceptors next year while Germany expands its own output under existing licenses.
Ukraine needs the interceptors to down Russian ballistic missiles that come several times per week. Each Russian attack on Kyiv costs the city budget about $12 million. More than four thousand buildings in Kyiv have been damaged by Russian strikes, with each attack adding to a repair bill the city carries alongside the human losses.

At least 12 people were killed overnight Monday into Tuesday in the first Russian airstrikes on Kyiv since the three-day ceasefire prompted by the visit of U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, authorities in the capital said.
Administrative buildings, warehouses, schools and residential buildings were damaged in six districts of Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. At least 10 people were injured.
The overnight attack extended beyond the Ukrainian capital to the Odesa region. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it "a complex strike" that "tried to plan to cause as much harm to life as possible."
Advertisement
Both Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered a pause on attacks on Moscow and Kyiv as Witkoff and Kushner traveled to both capitals for talks over the weekend.
"Please come more often, so that our people have the chance to live normally," the Ukrainian leader joked at a press conference with the U.S. envoys in Kyiv on Sunday.
"As soon as the U.S. presidential peace envoys left the city, Putin launched another massive and horrific attack on Kyiv," Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine Andrii Sybiha said on Tuesday. "[Putin's] ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy," the minister added.
On September 6, U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for the first time as Washington renewed its peace efforts, following talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
