articles.title: Korea’s Hanwha brings lasers and drones to Poland’s biggest defense show
articles.body:
- Hanwha Aerospace and Hanwha Systems are showcasing air defense, laser weapons, unmanned systems and artillery at MSPO 2026 in Poland, building on a partnership dating to 2014.
- Hanwha is pursuing a third K9 howitzer contract with Poland while already building Chunmoo missiles at a new Polish facility under a roughly $4 billion deal signed in December.
South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace and Hanwha Systems opened a joint exhibit at MSPO 2026 in Kielce, Poland, on September 8, presenting an expanded lineup of air defense, unmanned and artillery systems built around the company’s decade-long defense partnership with Warsaw.
The two companies are sharing a stand at the exhibition, which runs through September 11, under the slogan “Proven Partnership. Strategic Capabilities. Sovereign Defence.” Hanwha’s relationship with Poland dates back to 2014, when its K9 chassis was selected for the Polish Krab self-propelled howitzer, and has since expanded through the K9 howitzer program and the Chunmoo rocket launcher system, known in Poland as Homar-K.
The company’s newest offerings center on layered air defense. Hanwha is showing its L-SAM long-range surface-to-air missile launcher, the H-SHORAD short-range air defense system, the H-Shield counter-drone system, and a 40mm wheeled counter-UAS vehicle, all designed to link into Hanwha Systems’ command-and-control network alongside interceptor drones. Hanwha Systems is also displaying Cheon gwang, South Korea’s first operational laser weapon system, along with a 50-kilowatt laser mounted on an armored vehicle and a smaller 20-kilowatt tactical laser vehicle. The company says each laser shot costs roughly 2,000 South Korean won, or about $1.50, and can down a small drone within seconds.
On the ground, Hanwha is presenting its manned-unmanned teaming concept through a display combining the K9A1 howitzer with an unmanned rocket launcher and its H-UGV ground vehicle, an arrangement where the crewed howitzer provides firepower while unmanned systems handle reconnaissance and maneuver, keeping soldiers farther from direct fire. The stand also includes the export version of the K-NIFV infantry fighting vehicle and an active protection system meant to improve vehicle survivability. In the naval domain, Hanwha is showing unmanned surface vessels built for Baltic Sea operations, including the Striker-S, which pairs an unmanned boat with a Chunmoo rocket launcher.
Hanwha is also exhibiting the upgraded K9A2 howitzer alongside a new 155mm ammunition package that includes a trajectory-correcting fuze and a modular propellant charge system intended to improve accuracy. The company is pursuing a third execution contract with Poland for K9 howitzers, a follow-on to earlier deals that have made Poland one of the largest operators of the K9 family. Hanwha’s existing Homar-K contracts with Poland include a roughly $4 billion deal signed in December, covering Chunmoo CGR-080 guided missiles to be built at a dedicated production facility inside Poland, with deliveries beginning in 2030, part of a broader push to localize Korean weapons manufacturing on Polish soil. Hanwha is displaying four Chunmoo guided rocket variants at MSPO alongside maintenance tools including a predictive health-monitoring system and a K9 turret simulator.
On September 9, Hanwha Systems plans to publicly demonstrate a satellite-imagery analysis system for the first time, using artificial intelligence to process electro-optical, infrared and synthetic aperture radar imagery from satellites currently in operation, aiming to automate object detection and flag unusual activity for military analysts.
“Hanwha is proud to be a trusted defense and industrial partner in Poland,” said Jacek Cyrek, CEO of Hanwha Aerospace Europe. “At MSPO 2026, we are expanding our local footprint into air defense, MUM-T, and space AI, building true defense sovereignty and industrial capability together on Polish soil.”

articles.title: Sanctioned Russian ship Lady Mariia, tied to arms shipments, attacked by drones in the Mediterranean Sea
articles.body:
The Russian roll-on/roll-off cargo ship Lady Mariia (IMO: 9220641), which is under U.S. and Ukrainian sanctions, was attacked by drones in the Mediterranean Sea, according to the head of Ukraine’s Institute for Black Sea Strategic Studies, Andrii Klymenko, who reported that the vessel had been heading toward Syria.
Klymenko published footage of the attack, while a longer video was posted on the Telegram channel of Russian opposition commentator Alexander Nevzorov. The footage shows drones dropping munitions onto the vessel, with a fire breaking out after one explosion. Nevzorov claimed the Lady Mariia was hit 12 times and suggested that the drones had been launched by Ukrainian forces from the territory of Libya. He added that the ship was carrying Iranian weapons and armored vehicles intended for Russia.
Klymenko also hinted that the drones had been launched from Libyan territory, writing: “And it wasn’t us. Those were some nice, unknown drones from Libyan territory. What do we have to do with it?”
Ukrainian authorities have not officially commented on the attack. The number of hits, the origin of the drones, and the nature of the cargo on board have not been independently confirmed. The Ukrainian outlet UNITED24 Media also noted that claims about Iranian weapons and a Libyan launch point were based on Nevzorov’s reporting and had not been independently verified.
According to the vessel tracking platform Starboard Maritime Intelligence, the Lady Mariia left St. Petersburg in early August. The vessel passed through the Strait of Gibraltar on Aug. 29 and then called at the Algerian port of Oran. It later headed east across the Mediterranean. On the evening of Sept. 5, the Lady Mariia stopped transmitting its AIS (Automatic Identification System) signal.
Starboard Maritime Intelligence data also shows that since the spring of 2020, the Lady Mariia has made three calls at the Syrian port of Tartus and three at the Iranian ports of Bandar Abbas and Khorramshahr. The platform also recorded two calls at the Libyan port of Al-Buraika.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR) lists the Lady Mariia among the vessels that have been used to transport military cargo and weapons for Russia.
The ship is owned by the Russian company MG-Flot LLC, formerly known as Transmorflot. In May 2022, the U.S. imposed sanctions on Transmorflot and vessels linked to it. The Lady Mariia, which was previously named Stella-Maria, was also placed under U.S. restrictions. Ukraine imposed sanctions on the Lady Mariia on May 23, 2026.
According to HUR, MG-Flot is linked to Astrakhan businessman Dzhamaldin Pashayev, who built his business around the Port of Olya in Russia’s southern Astrakhan Region. The port is seen as one of Russia’s key logistics hubs for the International North-South Transport Corridor, which connects Russia with Iran.

articles.title: Ukrainian AI company after NATO competition: effectiveness of strikes on Russian airfields could increase tenfold
articles.body:
Ukrainian AI company after NATO competition: effectiveness of strikes on Russian airfields could increase tenfold
In a comment to Ukrinform, the company’s head, who uses the call sign Wild Cat, said the solution presented at the NATO competition would make strikes on enemy airfields many times more effective, as it represents an entirely new technological level.
“In short, our development is artificial intelligence for making the destruction of enemy airfields ten times more effective. It involves precision targeting of airfields, and the solution can be used both on UAVs and missiles,” the company head said.
He explained that Russia should not be underestimated, as it has one of the world’s best air defense systems, combined with one of the world’s best electronic warfare systems, which makes it considerably more difficult for Ukrainian forces to strike its airfields.
“Essentially, we are dealing with the protection of military airfields at a level that may not exist anywhere else in the world. Despite this, Ukraine is managing to effectively ‘reach’ Russian aircraft and helicopters at their airfields, both in Crimea and deep inside their territory,” Wild Cat said. At the same time, he believes that introducing the new development “will fundamentally change this situation.”
Read also: Ukrainian Forces Test New Robotic Turrets with Machine Guns on the Front Line
“This will help Ukraine significantly improve the effectiveness of strikes on enemy airfields,” the head of the Ukrainian company emphasized.
He noted that he had expected to win NATO’s Innovation Competition because he benchmarks his company against its main competitors in Ukraine and around the world, including the U.S. company Palantir Technologies, which develops artificial intelligence, including for Hornet “middle-strike” drones, “with which the Ukrainian side is currently wreaking havoc on the enemy’s logistics.”
According to him, Palantir remains stronger in the logistics sector, but the Ukrainian development has an advantage in airspace protection and operations against enemy airfields.
The company head said that winning the NATO competition represents recognition of the Ukrainian company’s solutions at the Alliance level.
“We are the only Ukrainian company to have won this competition. This means that our solution has been recognized as the best in this field across the Alliance. We are being invited to take part in further testing and trials, with the prospect of implementing our solutions at the NATO level. This is a huge boost for the company’s development and integration into the Alliance’s defense system,” he emphasized.
The head added that the company had been developing its technology since 2022 and had since collected, in his assessment, globally unique databases for training its artificial intelligence.
“No one else in the Western world has anything like this. And training data accounts for more than half of success,” the head of the Ukrainian AI company said.
Read also: Ukraine and Britain Sign Historic Artificial Intelligence Agreement
Wild Cat said that during the event, the company had also reached cooperation agreements with several other partners, including an agreement on joint production with a foreign company, as well as cooperation with a Ukrainian manufacturer. He added that since the company develops exclusively software modules, practical implementation of the solution requires cooperation with manufacturers of drones or missile systems.
The company head also said that a presentation of the solution at a training range was scheduled to take place within several weeks as part of an exercise. The next steps will include flight and combat trials, followed by the production of a small batch to identify shortcomings under real operating conditions, and only later full-scale production. According to the company head’s preliminary estimates, it should take between six and eighteen months for the development to enter combat use.
Regarding the financial prize in NATO’s Innovation Competition—the three winning companies will receive a total of €250,000—Wild Cat said it amounts to approximately 5–7% of the project’s current costs. However, he said the main value of the victory was not financial but reputational, providing an argument for potential investors and partners.
Assessing the development’s potential impact on the course of hostilities, the company head described it as “an ongoing confrontation between means and countermeasures.”
“We are now considering what the war will look like in two or three years. To some extent, we are already anticipating how the Russians will protect their airfields in the future—for example, they are already actively building bunkers for aircraft. We are developing the solution so that even these bunkers will not help them,” he emphasized.
The head of the AI company added that it had been working on strikes against enemy airfields since 2022, and that the current development takes into account its previous experience and the countermeasures Russia has attempted to use to reduce the effectiveness of Ukrainian attacks.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, NATO’s 19th Innovation Competition, organized by NATO’s Allied Command Transformation (ACT) and the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC), focused on persistent airfield denial . The Persistent Airfield Denial competition sought innovative technologies capable not only of damaging a military airfield but also of making it difficult for the enemy to restore its operations for an extended period.
The Ukrainian company took third place with an artificial intelligence-based solution for autonomous control of unmanned aerial vehicles. The technology enables operation without a constant connection to an operator, as well as the use of autonomous navigation and target recognition.
First place in the competition went to Czech company LPP Holding, which presented an autonomous long-range unmanned system capable of operating in conditions of active electronic warfare and without GPS navigation.
Second place went to Polish company Supercluster with its StratoAIM concept. The development involves using high-altitude balloons to launch autonomous gliding systems.

articles.title: Defense Forces neutralize 175 targets overnight, including 2 ballistic, 31 cruise missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defense Forces overnight into Tuesday, from 18:00 to 08:30, neutralized 175 enemy targets, including two ballistic missiles and 31 out of 32 cruise missiles; however, following the results of the night, missile and strike UAV impacts were recorded at 29 locations, the press service of the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:30, air defense shot down/suppressed 175 targets: 2 Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400/Onyx ballistic missiles; 31 Kh-101/Iskander-K cruise missiles; 142 enemy UAVs of the Shahed, Gerbera, and other drone types," reads the report by the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Telegram on Tuesday.
It is noted that the main directions of the attack were Odesa and Kyiv regions. Impacts of Russian missiles and strike UAVs were recorded at 29 locations, with falling debris from intercepted targets recorded at 9 locations.
The Air Force reported that the enemy attacked Ukraine with Onyx anti-ship missiles (from Bryansk, Kursk regions of Russia and occupied Crimea) and Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles (from Bryansk, Voronezh regions of Russia). The exact number of missiles for these types was not specified.
According to the Air Force, Ukraine was also attacked by 32 air-launched Kh-101 cruise missiles from Vologda region of Russia; 166 strike UAVs of the Shahed type (more than half of them jet-powered) and "Parodiya" decoy drones launched from Orel, Primorsko-Akhtarsk (Russia), occupied Donetsk, and Hvardiyske (occupied Crimea).
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, EW and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv as US envoys leave
articles.body:
Russia hits Kyiv after brief pause for US envoys' visit, killing two
Sept 8 - Russia pummelled Kyiv with drones and missiles early on Tuesday, resuming its air attacks after a brief halt for the visit of U.S. peace negotiators, killing two people and triggering fires across the Ukrainian capital.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko said 10 more had been injured in the city, while falling debris in one district caused fires at a five-storey apartment building and a three-storey residential block.
The attack damaged at least 14 high-rise buildings, a dorm, a school, a clinic, warehouses and other sites, officials said.
BRIEF RESPITE IN ATTACKS
Russia resumed its attacks after U.S. peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff left Kyiv following a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy on Sunday, as the Trump administration renewed its push to end Russia's 4-1/2-year war in Ukraine.
They arrived from talks in Moscow, after which the Kremlin said it did not rule out the resumption of the three-way negotiations.
"The moment the U.S. president's peace envoys left, (Russian President Vladimir) Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X.
"His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy," Sybiha said, urging allies to ramp up pressure on Moscow, as well as to provide interceptors to down ballistic missiles, since Kyiv's stocks of these run critically low.
Prior to the talks, Russia stepped up air attacks on Kyiv and nearby areas to nearly round-the-clock for several days, rather than mainly at night, using faster jet-propelled drones that killed residents and disrupted activities.
The Russian defence ministry said Moscow hit military and logistic targets in Kyiv and the surrounding region, as well as in the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk, Russian newswires said.
POLAND ACTIVATES AIRCRAFT
Amid explosions heard in Kyiv, neighbouring Poland, a NATO and European Union member, launched preventive operations against Russian missile attacks on Ukraine, the Polish army said.
Poland's Lublin airport has temporarily suspended flights because of the military operations.
In Russia, Ukrainian drones damaged civilian infrastructure and injured people in the Volga river city of Saratov, some 730 km (450 miles) southeast of Moscow, the regional governor said.
The area is home to a large oil refinery run by state oil company Rosneft, as well as other industrial and military facilities. REUTERS

articles.title: The least free place on earth: Occupied Ukraine
articles.body:
People play chess in a park in front of a sculpture reading "Russian Spring" in the Russian-occupied Crimean city of Sevastopol on July 22, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images
No political rights. No freedom of expression. No protection from secret detention without access to family, an attorney or a physician. No protection from deportation.
Welcome to Russia-occupied Ukraine.
For the second year running, U.S.-based democracy tracker Freedom House has listed Ukraine’s occupied eastern and southern territories as the most unfree places in the world — outranking South Sudan, North Korea and the Gaza Strip.
Advertisement
Inhabitants here are subject to repressive Russian legislation, including forcibly imposed citizenship and the use of antiterrorism laws against political dissidents and religious minority groups, Freedom House says. And it is this system of surveillance, repression, indoctrination and statetheft that pushes occupied Ukraine to the top of the list.
Discriminatory policies publicly encoded in Russian law permeate every aspect of residents’ lives — measures that appear to be changing the region’s demographics. Russia is “deliberately changing the ethnic composition so as to destroy a culture or tip the political balance in favor of another group,” the report notes.
International humanitarian law forbids any occupying power from introducing permanent changes to territories it occupies, particularly in demographic, social and economic domains. But Moscow claims these areas are not occupied — they are simply a part of Russia, and therefore subject to Russian law.
“This occupation is one of the most well-documented systems of repression, oppression and human rights violations because so much is put on the public record,” said Danielle Bell, head of the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission to Ukraine. “This is a systemic approach to restricting people’s rights and fundamental freedoms.”
The regime has “all the signs of cultural genocide,” said journalist Andrii Dikhtiarenko, a native of now-occupied eastern Ukraine.
Advertisement
From passportization to deportation
Starting from 2014, Russia has occupied about 20 percent of Ukraine in the country’s south and east — land Moscow calls “new historical territories.” And one of the processes aiding the Russification of these areas is passportization.
By officially designating Ukrainians living in Russia-occupied territories as “foreigners,” occupation authorities compel them to obtain Russian citizenship — which they can do through simplified procedures — in order to access essential rights, such as health care, social services, employment or property ownership.
For Liudmila Chub, it all began with her job. Speaking to POLITICO, Chub said that in 2023, she was told by her employer in Melitopol — located in the occupied Kherson region — that she had to obtain a Russian passport to keep working in his shop, or he would be fined. Chub went to the passport office, where she recorded an angry video about being forced to get a “chicken passport” — a dig at the two-headed Russian eagle emblem. The office’s security guard marched her straight to the occupation police.
A man waits for documentation to apply for a new Russian passport at a center in Melitopol in the Zaporizhzhia region in August 2022. | AFP via Getty Images
Chub spent the next eight months in detention in Kherson, with the courts regularly extending her arrest, alleging she was breaking military curfew. She was eventually given a statement to read out on camera, saying she did not want to live in Russia, then was allowed 15 minutes to collect items from her apartment and transported under armed guard to Russia’s border with Georgia.
Deported from the home she lived in her whole life, Chub still considers herself fortunate. She said others she encountered in prison had gone through the process of obtaining Russian citizenship only to be charged with spying or treason under Russian law, which carries huge sentences.
“They tie this passport to you, and then with it, they make you traitors to their country,” she said. “Everything in me was opposed to getting that passport, and it’s lucky I didn’t get it. That saved me.”
Advertisement
HRMMU has so far documented over 400 such detentions involving treason- and espionage-related charges in Russia-occupied territories, but it’s impossible to track numbers for incommunicado detention.
That is what happened to 59-year-old IT specialist Serhii Gryshchenkov from Sevastopol in occupied Crimea. After Russian security forces took him from his home in May 2025, Gryshchenkov’s family was unable to find out where he was, his daughter Darina told POLITICO. Her father, who did not hide his pro-Ukraine position, was held incommunicado and tortured for a year before eventually being charged with treason in June 2026, she said. The family does not know the details of the charges.
According to Darina, when her father reappeared in pretrial prison, he spoke of fellow prisoners who were still being secretly held after three or four years. “Their relatives don’t even know whether they are alive.”
One strategy encouraging demographic change in Ukraine’s occupied territories is the official confiscation of homes belonging to residents who fled the war, ensuring they cannot return.
Ukrainians who try to comply with this new rule and travel back home have fallen afoul of Russian “filtration,” faced with arrests and entry bans at Moscow’s Sheremetevo airport — the only possible entry point to get to occupied territories, as land borders are closed to them.
Journalist Olena — who was granted anonymity over security concerns regarding her relatives living under occupation — told POLITICO she had fled occupied Donetsk with her family in 2014. Helped by a sympathetic condominium manager, she had paid the utility bills for her own and her parents’ apartments for the next 12 years, hoping one day they could come home.
Later, Olena found out via occupation media that she had been publicly blacklisted as an “enemy.” Meanwhile, an acquaintance of hers was served a 50-year entry ban at Sheremetevo when trying to get back to her home in occupied Ukraine.
People dance at an outdoor bar in Sevastopol on July 22, 2026. | Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images
With this new law, “nothing can help us,” said Olena.
According to HRMMU monitoring, more than 60,000 private properties in occupied Ukraine have been identified as “ownerless” as of July this year. At least 6,500 of those properties have been expropriated, often given to veterans of Russia’s “special military operation” or sold to immigrants from Russia under preferential terms.
The effect of this has heavily impacted education in the region, with the introduction of a militarized Russian curriculum in schools. New textbooks teach the Kremlin’s official narrative that the occupied regions never supported Ukrainian independence and were always Russian. Parents who refuse to enroll their children in these schools, or enroll them in online Ukrainian education, are fined and threatened with losing parental rights.
These educational institutions can sometimes funnel students straight into the Russian armed forces. Once an individual holds a Russian passport — which the enforced system makes almost impossible to survive without — they can be drafted to fight against Ukraine. A practice that, like deportation, is explicitly prohibited by the Geneva Conventions.
The cumulative effect of all these measures has been the eradication of visible expressions of Ukrainian identity and wider dissent, said journalist Dikhtiarenko. “People who want to survive have to accept the rules of the game.”
Over at HRMMU, Bell’s worst fear is that the world will stop hearing about or noticing these violations. “When the climate becomes that coercive and that restrictive, and people are that silenced, that’s when we stop seeing the reports because people stop daring to speak out,” she said.
As more time passes, some inhabitants wonder whether there will be anything Ukrainian left, even if their home ever comes back under Kyiv’s control. However, despite their enforced Russian citizenship, Dikhtiarenko said the majority of residents still hold on to their Ukrainian passports, hiding them under floorboards or buried in the garden.

articles.title: Iran after 9/11
articles.body:
Sometimes, in the realm of what appears impossible, relief comes to the oppressed from an unexpected direction—almost as if from the unseen—when those who inflict oppression turn against one another. The Qur’an says: “And thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others because of what they used to earn.”(Qur’an 6:129)
In the light of such extraordinary turns of divine providence, there are moments when circumstances change so dramatically in favor of a weak and vulnerable party that its enemies—who apparently pose the greatest threat to it—find themselves arrayed against one another. They gradually weaken each other through their confrontation, and as a result of this struggle, the very nation that had appeared isolated and powerless begins to acquire strength. Then comes a moment when that nation turns around and launches such an unexpected blow against its adversary that the enemy is thrown into confusion and begins making statements so bewildered that the world can hardly resist mocking them. If the history of Iran over the past quarter-century is viewed from this perspective, the wars launched by the United States in Afghanistan and Iraq after 9/11 emerge as a remarkable example of this strange historical phenomenon.The Taliban established an extremely harsh and authoritarian system of government in Afghanistan, while Saddam Hussein’s Iraq was responsible for widespread  human-rights violations. At the same time, American policy in the Middle East and South Asia had for decades been characterized by wars, interventions, regime change, and the use of military force. But consider the strange irony of history: on the one hand, the Taliban were enemies of Iran; on the other, Saddam Hussein’s Iraq was Iran’s longstanding and bloody adversary. Then history took an extraordinary turn: on both fronts, Iran’s enemies became embroiled in wars with the United States.
 
 Iran did not start these wars. Yet, on the new strategic chessboard created by them, Iran arguably gained the greatest strategic advantage.This may be one of the most astonishing aspects of the post-9/11 era. To understand this story, however, we need to take several steps back. The Iranian Revolution of 1979 was not merely a political transformation for Iran. Following the overthrow of the Shah, Iran entered a revolutionary era that fundamentally altered its relationship with the major powers of the world. The United States became a bitter adversary of Iran, and Iran increasingly found itself isolated from the Western world. Barely a year after the Revolution, Saddam Hussein’s Iraq invaded Iran in 1980. Iran was plunged into a war that lasted almost eight years. Hundreds of thousands of people were killed, and Iran suffered enormous human and economic losses. Yet the Iranian state survived and maintained its sovereignty. But Iran’s security challenges were not confined to the West or Iraq. To its east, Afghanistan was also undergoing rapid transformation. Following the emergence of the Taliban, relations between Iran and the Taliban became extremely hostile. The two sides were divided by religious, political, and geopolitical differences. There was a profound ideological conflict between the Taliban’s rigid interpretation of Islam and Iran’s Islamic republican system.
In 1998, tensions reached a dangerous point. Taliban fighters seized the Iranian consulate in Mazar-i-Sharif and killed Iranian diplomats and a journalist who were present there. The incident provoked widespread outrage in Iran. Iranian forces massed near the Afghan border, and the two countries came extremely close to war. Thus, to Iran’s west stood Saddam Hussein’s Iraq, while to its east was Taliban-controlled Afghanistan. On one side was the country that had imposed an eight-year war on Iran; on the other was a force with which Iran had come close to armed conflict. Iran appeared to be trapped between two dangerous fronts.
Then history took a turn that perhaps even Tehran could not have imagined.
On September 11, 2001, al-Qaeda attacked the United States. The attack set the world’s greatest military power on a path toward war.The United States entered Afghanistan. The Taliban government was overthrown. And here history opened the first door for Iran, which had long appeared trapped in a geopolitical prison. The Taliban government, with which Iran had extremely hostile relations, was removed from power as a result of the American military intervention. But the greater surprise was yet to come.
If Afghanistan opened one door for Iran, Iraq opened a far larger strategic chapter. In 2003, the United States invaded Iraq. Saddam Hussein’s government was overthrown.
Here, the world witnessed a remarkable historical irony. Iran did not defeat Saddam Hussein. The United States did. Iran did not send American troops into Iraq. The United States did. Iran did not bomb Baghdad. The United States did. Yet when the war was over, the regional power that emerged strategically stronger and more secure was Saddam Hussein’s longtime enemy: Iran.
This is why former U.S. National Security Adviser Lieutenant General Brent Scowcroft once made the point that Iran had become a beneficiary of American activities in the Middle East, because the United States had eliminated one of Iran’s principal enemies. The significance of this admission lies in the fact that it came not from an Iranian analyst but from one of America’s most distinguished strategic thinkers. Scowcroft was not alone. Former U.S. President Barack Obama later identified Iran as the greatest regional beneficiary of the Iraq War. In his speech on August 5, 2015, defending the Iran nuclear agreement, Obama discussed the consequences of the Iraq War and stated: “The single greatest beneficiary in the region of that war was the Islamic Republic of Iran.” He immediately  explained why: “Iran… saw its strategic position strengthened by the removal of its longstanding enemy, Saddam Hussein.” For our purposes, this may be the most decisive American reference of all, because it came from a former U.S. president in an official address. American presidents, generals, senior diplomats, defense journalists, and leading foreign-policy experts have, in different words, acknowledged that the American wars in Iraq and Afghanistan strengthened Iran’s position. Here are some of the most significant observations on the subject. General Brent Scowcroft was a retired Lieutenant General in the U.S. Air Force and served as National Security Adviser to Presidents Gerald Ford and George H. W. Bush. When asked how much Iran benefited from the American invasion of Iraq and the overthrow of Saddam Hussein, he responded: “I don’t think there’s any question that Iran has been a beneficiary of our activities in the Middle East.” He then explained the reason:
 
 “One of their principal adversaries has been Iraq… we removed that enemy.”
This reference is particularly significant because it was not the assessment of a journalist or political activist. It came from a former senior U.S. military officer who had occupied one of the highest strategic positions in the American national-security establishment. Richard Haass, who served as Director of Policy Planning at the U.S. Department of State and later as President of the Council on Foreign Relations, described Iran as: “The great strategic beneficiary of the Iraq War.” He explained that he had already feared that after the destruction of Iraq: “Iran would benefit from no longer having a country like Iraq to offset it.” He later summarized the matter in an especially revealing sentence: “So Iran has been the great strategic gainer of the last couple of decades.” Peter W. Galbraith, a former U.S. Ambassador to Croatia and a former senior United Nations official in Afghanistan, wrote in The New York Review of Books: “Iran is the major beneficiary of the American-induced changes in Iraq since 2003.” Galbraith also said that following the overthrow of Saddam Hussein, Iranian-backed political and military forces entered the new Iraqi political order, resulting in a substantial expansion of Iranian influence. Thomas E. Ricks, a former military affairs reporter for The Washington Post and former editor of Foreign Policy, put it bluntly when he wrote about the Iraq War: “Iran has been the big winner in this war.” He later elaborated: “Iran has certainly done well, and is more powerful than it was in 2003.” David Petraeus was among the most important American military commanders during the Iraq War. In 2008, Bruce Riedel, a senior expert at the Brookings Institution, wrote that General Petraeus mentioned Iran 105 times during his congressional briefing, reflecting the reality that Iran had become an extraordinarily important power in the new Iraqi landscape.
Riedel’s article was titled: “Iraq, Petraeus, Iran: Coming to Grips with reality.” He wrote plainly that Petraeus’s briefing reflected the reality that: “Iran is the big winner of the American decision to invade and occupy Iraq.” CNN war correspondent Michael Ware similarly described the overall consequences of American military interventions by observing that the removal of Saddam Hussein—and, before that, the removal of the Taliban—both amounted in a sense to a “gift” to Tehran. There is also substantial American and Western evidence concerning Afghanistan. Here, however, an important distinction should be made. The evidence and statements concerning Iraq are much more explicit and numerous than those concerning Afghanistan. In the Afghan case, stronger evidence comes from policy analyses and U.S. government-linked institutions. The U.S. Institute of Peace’s Iran Primer, for example, described the removal of the Taliban after 9/11 as: “an unintended strategic gift from Washington.” Taken together, these references reveal a larger reality.
These were not fronts created by Iran. They were American wars. Yet history produced the extraordinary irony that the two major enemies whom the United States defeated on two major fronts were also two of Iran’s most significant regional adversaries. The Taliban fell in Afghanistan. Saddam Hussein fell in Iraq.
And, one after another, two major obstacles standing before Tehran were removed. This is where history poses a strange question: If the United States was an adversary of Iran, why did it eliminate two of Iran’s most important enemies? The answer is that wars do not always produce the results intended by those who launch them. A war may begin with one objective, yet its consequences may ultimately benefit an entirely different actor. America removed Iran’s enemies. Iran filled the resulting vacuum. Following Saddam Hussein’s overthrow, a new political order emerged in Iraq. Within this new system, Shiite political forces with historical, religious, and political ties to Iran rose to prominence. Iran took advantage of the opportunity. Its political influence in Iraq expanded. Its relations with Iraqi Shiite resistance groups strengthened. Baghdad became a far more accessible capital for Tehran. Iraq was no longer merely a neighboring country for Iran. It became an important component of Iran’s strategic depth.This would have been extremely difficult to imagine while Saddam Hussein remained in power. On one side were the enormous American sacrifices. On the other was Iran’s expanding influence.
Here we encounter one of the most bitter contradictions of the post-9/11 era for the United States. America spent almost two decades in Afghanistan and fought a prolonged war in Iraq. Thousands of American soldiers were killed. Trillions of dollars were spent.
The wars imposed enormous burdens on American society and the economy.
Meanwhile, Iran, without bearing anything remotely comparable in direct military costs, benefited from the regional vacuums created by these wars. It would, however, be inaccurate to claim that Iran became powerful solely because of the United States. Iran’s own statecraft, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, its regional alliances, its relationship with Hezbollah, its alliance with Syria, and its long-term geopolitical strategy were all fundamental sources of its power. Nevertheless, it cannot be ignored that the American wars created an environment in which Iran’s regional strategy acquired extraordinary room for expansion. Iran now confronted its adversaries from an entirely new strategic position. In January 2002, President George W. Bush famously designated Iran, Iraq, and North Korea as part of a so-called “Axis of Evil.” Yet only a year later, the United States invaded Iraq.
After that invasion, Saddam Hussein—once the dominant regional counterweight to Iran—was gone, while Iranian influence penetrated deeper into Iraq. History had, in effect, turned Washington’s own decision against its original strategic logic. What the United States may have hoped would help contain Iran instead created new geopolitical space for Iran. Then came Syria. After the outbreak of the Syrian conflict in 2011, Iran’s regional role became even more significant. Iran supported Bashar al-Assad’s government and maintained its influence through Hezbollah and other allied forces. Thus, Iraq became not merely an endpoint for Iran but a corridor. The chain of influence stretching from Iran through Iraq and Syria to Lebanon came to be viewed in subsequent years as part of Iran’s “strategic depth.” Here again, the indirect consequences of the post-9/11 era can be seen. The United States disrupted the old balance of power in a region, and Iran found space for itself within the new balance. Some may describe this simply as geopolitics. Others may regard it as an accident of history. And still others may see it as one of those extraordinary turns of providence in which the enemies of a weaker nation end up fighting one another. Whatever interpretation one chooses, the outcome remains striking.
Today, Iran has reached a point where it stands directly against an American power that the world has long regarded—or once regarded—as among the greatest military powers on Earth. And Israel, despite possessing a nuclear arsenal, has not been able to subdue Iran with ease. Even if one does not describe this as an American defeat, it is difficult to deny the reality that Iran has not fled the battlefield. Instead, it has remained standing in confrontation with a military power vastly greater than itself. This is a position that few could perhaps have imagined for the weak, isolated, and war-ravaged Iran of the years immediately following 1979.
After 9/11, the United States launched a massive war against terrorism perpetrated by the very extremists whose terrorism had helped trigger the conflict. The objective was to make America safer and eliminate its enemies. But history’s ledger contains another extraordinary result: After punishing Afghanistan and Iraq, the United States ultimately wanted to turn Iran into the “Venezuela” of the region. Yet after the World Trade Center collapsed, the measures America undertook in the name of its own security contributed, paradoxically, to making Iran more stable, more influential, and more strategically resilient. This is perhaps the greatest paradox of the post-9/11 era. On the 25th anniversary of 9/11, we should not ask only: Why was America attacked on September 11? We should also ask another question: Who ultimately gained the greatest geopolitical advantage from the wars that the United States launched after that attack? And if we return to the philosophy of history and divine providence with which we began this story, perhaps we can conclude in these words: Sometimes no angel descends from the heavens to rescue the weak. Instead, circumstances bring their enemies face to face with one another. And the story of Iran over the past nearly half-century is a striking example of this extraordinary reality: The enemies that Iran might have exhausted itself fighting were, in the course of history, made to fight one another. And when the dust settled, Iran was standing stronger than before.
That may be the most astonishing lesson of the history that unfolded after 9/11.
By Professor Tanveer Haider Naqvi

articles.title: Brussels cleared Ukraine to spend EU loan money on American Patriot missiles for the coming winter of Russian attacks
articles.body:
The European Commission has approved Ukraine's request to buy US-made Patriot interceptor missiles with money from the European Union's €90 billion ($105 billion) loan, an EU official told Suspilne. Kyiv filed the application four days earlier and asked for more than €2 billion ($2.3 billion). The decision settles who pays, not when the missiles arrive.
Brussels signed off four days after the request
Ukraine submitted the application on 3 September under the Ukraine Support Loan program. The Commission said at the time it was working to clear it in the shortest possible period.
Kyiv asked for the money to buy interceptors, and it falls under the EU credit line for 2026 and 2027. That sum can buy anywhere from about 190 to 580 interceptors, depending on the price Washington sets.
Trump’s peace envoys left, and Russia hit Kyiv with ballistics—the one thing Ukraine still struggles to stop
What the €90 billion covers
The European Council decided to create the loan in December 2025, and the Council of the EU finalized the financing mechanism in April 2026. Hungary's veto held the package up for months before it cleared, and Ukraine's parliament then accepted a wartime tax overhaul to unlock the first tranche.
About €30 billion ($35 billion) of the total goes to economic support and €60 billion ($70 billion) to military needs and defense capabilities. The EU raises the money by borrowing on international capital markets against guarantees from its own budget.
Why European money buys American missiles
The military half of the program funds arms purchases, Ukrainian and European defense industry in particular. It also allows purchases outside the bloc when European producers cannot supply enough of what Ukraine needs.
On 6 August the Commission confirmed Ukraine may use loan money for interceptors, noting that Kyiv defines its own requirements and files the applications. That opened the door to non-European weapons. Nothing in Ukraine's inventory stops Russian ballistic missiles without Patriot interceptors, as Russia showed in August by hitting Kyiv and the Boryspil airport hub twice inside a day.
Ukraine's interceptor arithmetic
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine agreed with the US on monthly interceptor deliveries, while calling the volumes short of what the country needs. He put the winter requirement at no less than about 5% of American output of these missiles.
A shortage of allied Patriot missiles, combined with heavier Russian strikes, made July the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022, according to UN figures.

articles.title: Russia resumes deadly strikes on Kyiv after pause for Trump envoys’ visit
articles.body:
Russia resumes deadly strikes on Kyiv after pause for Trump envoys’ visit
Explosions rock Ukrainian capital after expiration of a three-day halt for Witkoff and Kushner visit
Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv overnight, killing two people and sending smoke billowing above the Ukrainian capital, ending Moscow’s temporary halt to strikes on the city.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered the pause in attacks as US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the Russian and Ukrainian capitals at the weekend.
Fresh explosions early Tuesday triggered fires and sent locals down into basements and metro stations for shelter.
“The moment the US president’s peace envoys left, Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv, damaging residential areas and killing at least two people,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said on social media.
“His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy.”
Witkoff and Kushner’s trips provided no immediate breakthrough in ending the four-and-a-half-year war, but represented Washington’s re-engagement with trying to broker a deal between the two sides, which had been on hold for months.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says US exploring steps to de-escalate Russia-Ukraine war as Russian attacks continue
articles.body:
The US is exploring possible steps for Ukraine and Russia to de-escalate the war during the winter while restarting negotiations toward a broader peace agreement, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Axios news site, as Russia resumed strikes on Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said on Monday that the weeks ahead could provide an opportunity for diplomacy, arguing that Russian President Vladimir Putin may be seeking to avoid antagonising US President Donald Trump ahead of US midterm elections.
"My feeling (is) that Putin needs Trump," he said. "He doesn't want ... to upset him."
Asked whether Putin might seek to give Trump a diplomatic achievement before the elections, Zelenskyy replied: "Yeah."
Zelenskyy met on Sunday in Kiev with Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner following their three-hour meeting with Putin in Moscow.
He said they conveyed that "the Russians are ready to negotiate," while noting, however, that Russia's battlefield actions and intensified attacks do not indicate a willingness to compromise.
Still, he said his understanding was that Putin is "ready to discuss" ideas aimed at advancing negotiations.
New proposals
Zelenskyy said the US team travelled to Moscow and Kiev primarily to "unblock" the diplomatic process and brought new proposals, including possible measures to reduce tensions ahead of and during winter.
"There are ideas around energy (facilities) and around grain (shipments), around electricity (facilities) and around oil and gas (exports). We have different interests, Russia and we," Zelenskyy said.
He said the emerging US approach appeared to involve both restarting negotiations and finding arrangements that could prevent a major escalation during winter, calling that interpretation "very close to the reality of these conversations."
The aim, he said, would be to identify steps "which can bring (the) sides closer to peace."
Zelenskyy said Washington also supports a separate winter assistance package for Ukraine involving air defence and energy support.
"It's not only about missiles," he said. "It's also about LNG (liquefied natural gas) ... and it's also about steps of de-escalation."
Zelenskyy said Kiev wants to use September and October to revive diplomacy, with the UN General Assembly in New York later this month potentially providing an opportunity for further US-Ukraine discussions. He also said another trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia meeting remained possible.
"We have this September, October to find any way to speak," he said. "Without dialogue … we will not have (a) result."
Russian attacks continue
Meanwhile, a series of "strong" explosions rang out in Kiev, AFP news agency journalists said early on Tuesday, as Russia resumed strikes on the Ukrainian capital after a three-day halt.
The explosions triggered car alarms in the city centre, the journalists said, after the Kiev city military declared an air raid alert.
In the wider Kiev region, the State Emergency Service said Russian forces launched drone strikes targeting Boryspil and Fastiv districts.
The attacks ignited fires at industrial enterprises in the Boryspil area, where a blaze destroyed seven trucks. Rescuers also responded to a logistics complex that was struck twice, successfully extinguishing all fires at the scene.
Kiev Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed that the capital was under a ballistic attack, calling for medics to the city's Solomianskyi district, No official information is currently available regarding deaths or injuries resulting from the attacks.

articles.title: Poland unveils its new heavy infantry fighting vehicle
articles.body:
- PGZ unveiled its new CBWP heavy infantry fighting vehicle in full for the first time at MSPO 2026, built by subsidiary Huta Stalowa Wola.
- The vehicle is armed with the ZSSW-30 turret already used on Poland's Rosomak and Borsuk vehicles, and Poland aims to have a running prototype by the end of 2026.
Poland’s state-owned defense conglomerate PGZ unveiled its new heavy infantry fighting vehicle in full for the first time at MSPO 2026, the Kielce arms fair, after days of teasing only partial glimpses of the vehicle on social media.
The vehicle, known by its Polish designation CBWP, or Ciężki Bojowy Wóz Piechoty, was developed by Huta Stalowa Wola, a PGZ subsidiary that builds much of Poland’s tracked armored equipment. PGZ described the vehicle as combining a high level of crew protection, strong mobility and firepower delivered through the ZSSW-30 remote-controlled turret.
The ZSSW-30 is already in Polish service, mounted on the Rosomak wheeled armored personnel carrier and the lighter, amphibious Borsuk infantry fighting vehicle. Developed by Huta Stalowa Wola together with Polish electronics firm WB Group, the turret carries a 30mm Bushmaster automatic cannon, a coaxial 7.62mm machine gun and twin launchers for Spike-LR anti-tank guided missiles, and is built around a hunter-killer targeting concept that lets the vehicle commander search for new threats while the gunner engages one already found.
PGZ and Huta Stalowa Wola signed a framework agreement with Poland’s Armament Agency in August 2023 covering the supply of several hundred heavy infantry fighting vehicles in various configurations, along with a logistics and training package. Under that agreement, the vehicle’s chassis draws on the design used for Poland’s Krab self-propelled howitzer. The vehicle is intended to carry a three-person crew and eight dismounted soldiers, engaging armored and unarmored targets, exposed weapon positions and field fortifications while providing fire support to infantry in direct contact with the enemy, in any weather, day or night.
Huta Stalowa Wola previously showed a model of the vehicle, under the name Ratel, at MSPO 2025. That version was described as a roughly 40-tonne design fitted with the Obra-3 laser warning and protection system, a nuclear, biological and chemical protection suite, and the option to add an active protection system, with room for six to eight dismounted troops behind a two-person crew. Poland has said it is targeting a running prototype of the new chassis by the end of 2026, to be followed by qualification trials, ballistic testing, mine-resistance evaluation and formal assessment against the military’s requirements.
The vehicle’s front armor is believed to be designed to resist 30x173mm armor-piercing cannon rounds fired from 500 meters, a protection level consistent with STANAG 4569 Level 6, and its hull design reportedly leaves room to add explosive reactive armor, including Poland’s own modular Pangolin system, for additional protection against anti-tank warheads.

articles.title: Germany plans “Cyberdome” and mobile anti-drone units after Leipzig airport sabotage attempt
articles.body:
Germany’s Interior Ministry is preparing a package of measures to protect the country from Russian drone attacks, computer network intrusions, and acts of sabotage, according to a Bild report citing Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt. The measures are being developed following an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August, which Berlin has blamed on Russia.
Dobrindt’s plan calls for expanding the federal police mobile anti-drone units. Teams equipped with helicopters and specialized vehicles are expected to be based in Frankfurt, Munich, Hamburg, Berlin, Stuttgart, Düsseldorf, Leipzig, Hanover, and Cologne.
They would be tasked with protecting airports, train stations, and other major transport hubs, along with Berlin’s government district. In addition to intercepting drones, the units would be responsible for defusing bombs and other explosive devices.
Operators of critical infrastructure — including water and energy companies, as well as defense plants — would also be given the authority to counter drones on their own. The proposed powers would allow them not only to detect drones but also to actively repel attacks.
Dobrindt told Bild that Russian hybrid attacks had become an everyday reality. He cited the facts of drones carrying explosives, agent activity, network intrusions, and acts of sabotage.
Another part of the plan would expand the use of artificial intelligence, biometric facial recognition, and video surveillance at train stations and other locations. The technologies would be used to identify people preparing attacks or espionage operations and to automatically detect weapons and suspicious behavior.
To counter cyberattacks, the German authorities plan to create a national system called “Cyberdome,” which Bild described as a network of digital sensors designed to detect and repel attempts to break into government and corporate systems.
In early August, Leipzig/Halle Airport temporarily suspended operations after a drone with a detonator was found near a Ukrainian An-124 transport aircraft. A separate cargo plane was diverted to Hanover due to the closure and struck an unidentified object while still near Leipzig; police found damage to the front of the aircraft after it landed.
Investigators later identified two individuals that it suspects participated in preparations for the attack: a Russian-born man carrying a Latvian passport and a Belarus-born man who holds a Russian passport.
German investigators believe the first man organized logistics and acted as an instructor. The second was identified through traces of DNA found both on the drone and on an antenna near the airport. Three drones, either intact or in pieces, were eventually discovered at the scene.
On Sept. 1, the German government formally accused Russia of organizing the attack, citing the results of its police investigation and intelligence findings. Berlin said that in response to the incident it would close Russia’s consulate general in Bonn effective Sept. 18, terminate an agreement governing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin, and tighten entry controls for Russian citizens.
The Russian authorities rejected the accusations, calling the incident a “provocation.”
On Aug. 28, a collection of European countries bordering the Baltic Sea said they planned to create a task force to counter drones and other hybrid threats. At a meeting in Flensburg, Dobrindt said the group was intended to ensure rapid information sharing. The initiative followed a wider rise in drone sightings near European airports, as well as sabotage incidents involving undersea cables and gas pipelines.

articles.title: Brazil’s cruise missile testing resumes after years of delay
articles.body:
- Avibras Aeroco and the Brazilian Army successfully test-fired the MTC-300 cruise missile on August 26, resuming certification testing after a roughly four-year pause.
- The missile can strike targets up to 300 kilometers away, and Brazil's army has also revived plans for an upgraded Block II version with improved range and guidance.
Brazil’s Avibras Aeroco and the Brazilian Army completed a successful test launch of the country’s first indigenous cruise missile on August 26, a milestone in a certification process that stalled for roughly four years while the missile’s manufacturer worked through a severe financial crisis.
The test took place at the Army Evaluation Centre’s Marambaia Test Range in Rio de Janeiro, according to a joint statement from Avibras Aeroco and the Brazilian Army. The missile, known as the Tactical Cruise Missile or MTC, is part of the ASTROS artillery system’s family of guided munitions and is designed to strike targets up to 300 kilometers (186 miles) away. The companies said the exercise met all objectives set for this phase of testing.
The MTC-300, also called the AV-MTC 300, has a range of 300 kilometers, a diameter of 450 millimeters and a length of 5.4 meters (17.7 feet). Each ASTROS launch unit currently in Brazilian Army service can carry two of the missiles. The system uses a combination of satellite and inertial navigation to hit within roughly 30 meters of its target, and Brazil has designed two warhead options for it: a high-explosive version and a cluster configuration carrying 66 submunitions. A turbojet engine built by Brazilian company Turbomachine, producing up to 499 kilograms-force (1,100 pounds-force) of thrust, propels the missile to high subsonic speeds of around 1,000 km/h (620 mph) at cruising altitudes between 200 and 800 meters.
Brazil’s army and Avibras began developing the missile in 2012 under the ASTROS Strategic Programme, intending to give the country’s rocket artillery system enough range to strike well beyond its immediate region. Testing stalled in 2022, when Avibras fell into a financial crisis tied to roughly 800 million reais ($133 million) in debt, triggering a prolonged strike involving around 900 employees and effectively freezing the company’s defense programs. The situation began to turn around in May, when Avibras reached an agreement to settle its outstanding labor debts, clearing the way for the company’s restructuring under the new name Avibras Aeroco and the resumption of missile testing.
According to the Brazilian Army, the August test served as part of the missile’s final flight-verification testing, ahead of a last remaining test that will use a live warhead, the final step required before the MTC-300 can be formally validated for service.
Brazil’s army has also revived plans for an upgraded version of the missile, known as MTC Block II, according to guidelines the army published in August for its broader ASTROS-FOGOS Strategic Programme. The Block II upgrade calls for adding an unspecified terminal guidance system, extending the missile’s range and improving its warhead, changes the army has linked to new requirements for coastal defense and for striking moving targets, a description that suggests the upgraded missile could eventually engage ships. The Block II project remains officially listed as “not started.”
Officials attending the August test included Brig. Gen. João Paulo Zago, head of the Army Evaluation Centre; Brig. Gen. Marcelo Gurgel do Amaral Silva, manager of the army’s FOGOS Strategic Programme; and Brig. Gen. Moisés da Paixão Junior, manager of the Field Artillery Sub-programme, alongside representatives from the Army Projects Office, the Manufacturing Directorate, the Military Institute of Engineering and the Army Technology Centre.
Avibras’s pause since 2022 gave rise to competition it did not previously face in Brazil’s missile industry. Other Brazilian firms have since disclosed their own cruise missile programs, including the AATD, reported to have a range of up to 2,000 kilometers (1,240 miles) using the same turbojet engine as the MTC-300, and the MCX, described as an export-friendly medium-range cruise missile with a satellite datalink. Separately, Brazilian company SIATT integrated Brazil’s MANSUP anti-ship missile onto Marine Corps ASTROS launchers in 2025, despite legal action from Avibras at the time, and is developing its own coastal defense missile system.

articles.title: France, Italy Working on SAMP/T Delivery as Allies Explore More Patriot Systems for Ukraine
articles.body:
European countries are exploring ways to quickly send additional Patriot air defense systems to Ukraine ahead of winter, while France and Italy are working together to provide Kyiv with a SAMP/T system and Aster missiles, sources at the French presidential palace told Ukrinform.
The discussions come as Ukraine seeks to strengthen its air defenses ahead of another winter of Russian strikes on critical and civilian infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Countries that manufacture or have already purchased Patriot systems are considering several options,” the Élysée Palace said when asked whether additional Patriot systems could be delivered to Ukraine soon.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has been particularly insistent on strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses as Russia changes its tactics and weapons used in attacks, according to the sources.
Patriot systems could address part of Ukraine’s needs, but Kyiv also requires other air defense systems, the sources said.
France has already announced that, in coordination with Italy, it plans to provide Ukraine with a SAMP/T system currently in French possession, along with Aster missiles.
“They will effectively strengthen the protection of Ukrainian cities,” the Élysée sources said.
Asked when the systems and missiles would be delivered, the French presidential palace said only: “The work is ongoing.”
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 7, 2026
The coming winter is expected to be difficult for Ukraine because of continued Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure.
“Everyone understands that the winter will be difficult,” the French sources said, while stressing that Russia has not achieved a breakthrough on the battlefield.
“There is no scenario in which the Russians would manage to break through the front line,” they said.
“Their strikes on cities cause significant damage and have a dramatic impact on the civilian population, but on the battlefield, the Russians are not making a breakthrough.”
The French sources said continued military and financial support for Ukraine, alongside increased pressure on Russia, would be necessary under the circumstances.
Zelensky said earlier that Ukraine’s leadership would soon consider the development of the joint FREYJA anti-ballistic program, as well as additional long-range strike capabilities.

articles.title: ‘Unpredictable Times’: Finland Fortifies NATO Frontier with 200-km Russia Border Fence
articles.body:
Finland has completed a 200-kilometer fence along selected sections of its border with Russia, as Helsinki strengthens its eastern frontier against what it sees as a growing security threat from Moscow.
The Finnish Border Guard marked the completion of the barrier at the Nuijamaa border crossing in southeastern Finland on Monday, capping a project conceived after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine reshaped the Nordic country’s security policy.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The state’s most important duty is to see to the safety of its nationals,” Interior Minister Mari Rantanen said at the event.
“The eastern border fence is a necessary part of an effective border surveillance system in these unpredictable times,” she added.
The fence covers selected sections of Finland’s 1,340-kilometer frontier with Russia – the longest border Russia shares with any EU or NATO member.
Rantanen said Finland could eventually extend the barrier and called for additional EU funding to help eastern member states strengthen their borders.
The 200-kilometer barrier consists of dozens of separate sections concentrated in areas deemed most vulnerable.
The system includes a 4.5-meter-high fence, technical surveillance equipment, patrol roads and a 25-meter-wide cleared strip along the frontier. The project cost €356 million.
What to Make of Witkoff and Kushner’s Return to Russia-Ukraine Peace Talks
                                                                                                                                                                         
From non-alignment to NATO
Finnish political parties agreed in October 2022 on the need to build a partial fence along the Russian frontier, months after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Pilot sections were built in 2023, with large-scale construction beginning in 2024.
The decision came amid a historic shift in Finland’s security policy. The country joined NATO in April 2023, ending decades of military non-alignment in response to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The fence took on added importance after Helsinki accused Russia of facilitating the movement of migrants toward its border in late 2023 as a form of hybrid pressure.
Around 1,000 asylum seekers from third countries arrived at the frontier from Russia that autumn, prompting Helsinki to progressively shut its eastern border crossings before closing them all in December.
Russia denied orchestrating the influx.
Border crossings to remain shut
Rantanen said on Monday the crossings would remain closed, citing the continuing war in Ukraine and concerns over Moscow’s hybrid operations.
“The border crossings with Russia will not be opened because the security situation related to the military attack on Ukraine and hybrid operations has not changed,” she said.
The fence is part of a broader push by Finland to bolster its preparedness amid heightened security concerns over Russia.
Last week, more than 2,000 people took part in a two-day drill in the central city of Kuopio, billed as Europe’s largest civil defense exercise since the end of World War II.
The drill tested how authorities and civilians would respond to cyberattacks, disruptions to electricity and water supplies, and the threat of missile strikes from Russia.

articles.title: Iran conveys its ‘conditions’ to US – source
articles.body:
Iran conveys its ‘conditions’ to US – source
Iran has conveyed its conditions to the US through intermediaries after Washington recently sent new proposals to Tehran, a political source in the Iranian capital has told RT.
The reported contacts come amid renewed regional efforts to revive diplomacy after last week’s flare-up, when the US carried out several rounds of strikes on Iran and Tehran retaliated with missile and drone attacks on American military facilities in Jordan and Bahrain.
“Following the halt of negotiations resulting from US breaches of commitments and its repeated failures in military engagements, the US has recently conveyed proposals to Tehran through mediators,” the source said.
Given Washington’s “repeated violations” and “constant fluctuations in its positions,” Tehran responded by conveying its own conditions to the intermediaries, the source added.
The source did not disclose the details of either the American proposals or the Iranian conditions, but said mediators “continue to talk to both parties.”
Tehran has been pushing Washington to honor the commitments outlined in the June Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), but the US is now reportedly seeking a new, broader agreement covering both the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s nuclear program, the Financial Times reported last week.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said on Monday that US and Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities were themselves the main obstacle to inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), arguing that Washington was responsible for the resulting lack of access while simultaneously using the issue to increase pressure on Tehran.
“The ball has long been in the US court,” Baqaei said, adding that Washington must end its military attacks, economic sanctions and naval blockade if it wants to resolve the confrontation.
“Diplomacy is a dynamic and continuous process,” the spokesman said, noting that delegations from Oman and Pakistan have visited Iran in recent weeks, while Qatari representatives held talks with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Tehran on Sunday.
Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari told CNN that Doha had put forward several ideas and was exploring different scenarios aimed at addressing the concerns of both sides.
Tehran and Muscat have meanwhile reported significant progress on a separate arrangement for a temporary safe shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials have stressed, however, that such an agreement would not amount to the full reopening of the strategic waterway, as Washington has claimed.

articles.title: Ukraine Names Hanna Hvozdiar Deputy Defense Minister to Scale Arms Production
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Cabinet of Ministers appointed Hanna Hvozdiar deputy defense minister on Tuesday, Sept. 8, tasking her with scaling up weapons production and expanding exports as Kyiv races to arm its front lines faster.
Hvozdiar will oversee Ukraine’s defense industry, the defense ministry wrote, inviting the ex-CEO of Ukraine’s largest military charity fund, Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation, back in the ministry’s offices.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The appointment is part of a broader effort to strengthen the ministry’s team for developing Ukraine’s defense industry and speeding up supplies to the front, the agency wrote in its press release.
“Our task is a strong Ukrainian defense industry that gives the front what it needs now and creates a long-term advantage for Ukraine,” the press release quoted Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara.
The ministry named front-line supply as the top priority for Hvozdiar’s work, saying Ukrainian soldiers must receive enough domestically made weapons on time and in sufficient quantity to counter Russian threats on the battlefield, which will require manufacturers to increase output and gain more capacity to scale.
A separate focus for Hvozdiar will be exporting Ukrainian defense products whose output exceeds front-line needs, an area the ministry wrote could help build mutually beneficial partnerships with Ukraine’s allies and attract additional financing for the country’s defense.
175 Targets Down, But Ballistic Missiles Still Get Through
The defense ministry said it will work toward predictable and clear rules for producers, continue direct dialogue with the defense industry, and create conditions for scaling up production.
Hvozdiar previously served as deputy defense minister from July 2025 to January 2026, after which she worked as advisor to the minister. Before that, from September 2023 to July 2025, she was deputy minister for strategic industries, where her projects included launching Zbroya, Ukraine’s only online platform for weapons manufacturers.
Prior to entering government, Hvozdiar worked at the Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation, serving as deputy director in 2021-22 before leading the foundation in 2022-23.
