articles.title: Iran warns South Korea against military role in Persian Gulf
articles.body:
Iran warns South Korea against military role in Persian Gulf
TEHRAN — Iran has warned South Korea against any military involvement in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz, while accusing Washington of creating disruption in regional shipping and rejecting Western efforts to revive international pressure over Tehran’s nuclear program.
The warnings, delivered by Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Monday, came as Tehran sought to reinforce its position on three increasingly intertwined issues: security in the Strait of Hormuz, the continuing confrontation with the United States and Israel, and international efforts to exert pressure on Iran through the International Atomic Energy Agency and the United Nations.
In a Korean-language post on X, Baqaei highlighted the long-standing relationship between Tehran and Seoul but drew a sharp distinction between economic and diplomatic ties and military cooperation with the United States.
Iran and South Korea have maintained diplomatic relations for more than six decades, he said, adding that Tehran values its traditionally friendly relations with Seoul. But under current circumstances, he warned, any operational military participation by South Korea in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz would be viewed by Iran as direct support for an aggressor.
Baqaei argued that Iran is currently defending itself against 'US aggression and attacks on Iranian civilians.' Against that backdrop, he said, the deployment or participation of foreign military forces in the strategic waterway could carry serious consequences.
He also rejected the idea that sovereign states should respond to US pressure by joining military operations against Iran, saying that no responsible government should submit to coercion to participate in aggression.
Baqaei separately accused Washington of attempting to shift responsibility for disruptions to commercial shipping and rising energy prices onto Iran, arguing that the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz was triggered by the US and Israel.
In a post on X, he said the waterway had remained open until February 28, when the United States and Israel launched their military campaign against Iran.
Baqaei said the conflict had disrupted commercial shipping, halted tankers, and contributed to higher energy prices. He accused Washington of attempting to portray the resulting economic consequences as a cost imposed on the international community by Iran.
Iran warns against renewed nuclear pressure
Baqaei also rejected efforts by the United States and Israel to pressure IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi and advance a move to refer Iran's nuclear file to the UN Security Council.
He criticized a draft resolution based on a recent IAEA report, arguing that Western governments had repeatedly turned to nuclear watchdog when they were unable to achieve their political objectives through other means.
He also challenged the legal rationale being advanced by Western governments over the so-called snapback mechanism, under which previous UN Security Council sanctions could potentially be restored.
According to Baqaei, Western governments' current actions contradict their own interpretation of the mechanism and effectively reinforce the position previously taken by Iran, China and Russia that the mechanism is not applicable in the present circumstances.
He also accused the three European powers involved in the process of having lost credibility with Tehran and described some of their demands as unreasonable.
The spokesman placed particular responsibility on Washington for the current impasse over IAEA access to Iranian nuclear facilities. He argued that US and Israeli military actions had created the circumstances that prevented normal cooperation between Iran and the Agency.
Baqaei warned that Tehran would respond to any new action against it, describing the latest diplomatic pressure as evidence of hostile intentions and an effort to further escalate tensions.
Iran accuses US of deliberately targeting civilians
Responding to questions about attacks on civilian sites, Baqaei said Iran would continue to hold the United States accountable for violations of international humanitarian law.
He cited several incidents, including a deadly attack on a wedding ceremony on Iran's Sirik Island, as examples of a broader pattern of attacks against civilians.
Baqaei questioned how US forces, which possess highly accurate weapons, could have failed to identify civilian locations such as a school in Minab, a stadium in Lamerd or the wedding venue in Sirik.
Iran, he said, should not allow such incidents to disappear into history without accountability.
Tehran credits Oman with good faith on Hormuz talks
Against the backdrop of the confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran also offered a comparatively positive assessment of Oman's role in recent discussions concerning maritime security.
Baqaei said Oman had acted in good faith during talks with Iran on shipping security and emphasized the importance of the interests of the two littoral states.
Oman, he noted, is a neighboring coastal country with longstanding and close relations with Iran and has played a constructive role throughout the process.
At the same time, Baqaei cautioned that the outcome of the next stages remained uncertain.
He said an understanding between Iran and Oman was necessary for securing shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz, but by itself would not be sufficient to resolve the broader security crisis.

articles.title: Huawei heads to trial in US over its business dealings in Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Huawei heads to trial in US over its business dealings in Iran
Eight years after US prosecutors secretly charged China's Huawei Technologies with defrauding HSBC and other banks over its business with Iran, the case is finally heading for trial.
Huawei also faces charges for conspiring to steal trade secrets from five US technology companies, and is accused of lying about its dealings in North Korea and supplying surveillance equipment to Iran to track protesters during 2009 anti-government demonstrations in Tehran. Jury selection is expected to begin on Tuesday in federal court in Brooklyn, New York.
The trial will bring to a close one of the US government's earliest and most closely watched battles against a Chinese company, and will play out as tech competition heats up between the two countries and Washington seeks to prevent American technology from aiding Beijing's military. The US-China tech war has now spread across multiple technology sectors, including artificial intelligence.
The saga began in 2018 with the arrest of Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou in Vancouver, which sparked a diplomatic crisis involving the United States, China and Canada.
Convictions on the Iran-related charges would bolster Washington's case for having placed Huawei, one of China's leading technology companies, on a US trade blacklist in 2019, citing alleged criminal conduct that threatened national security.
The trial before US District Judge Ann Donnelly is expected to last about three months and overlap with Chinese President Xi Jinping's September 24 meeting with President Donald Trump in Washington. Potential jurors have filled out 27-page questionnaires, including about their views on China's and Iran's governments.
Other charges include violating US sanctions against Iran, money laundering, racketeering, wire fraud and obstruction. Huawei has pleaded not guilty on all charges and denied any wrongdoing.
The criminal case is based in part on reporting by Reuters in 2012 and 2013 about close ties between Huawei and Skycom, a firm that operated in Iran.
Reuters reported that Skycom had offered to sell at least €1.3 million ($1.5 million) worth of embargoed Hewlett-Packard computer equipment to Iran's largest mobile-phone operator in 2010. Reuters also reported that Meng had served on Skycom's board of directors between February 2008 and April 2009. The coverage can be read here and here.
Beijing has long criticized the case, saying it was part of a bigger campaign against China's technological rise. A Huawei spokesperson said in a statement on Saturday, "The government's overarching narrative is demonstrably false."
Today Huawei is a centerpiece of China's AI chip ambitions, and has diversified beyond network gear and smartphones. It has described the criminal case as an effort to undermine its competitiveness and the theft accusations as a repackaging of long-resolved commercial disputes.
If Huawei is convicted, prosecutors will seek the forfeiture of property or proceeds obtained from its illegal activity.
The case against the company was brought during the first Trump administration, which also took actions to curb the use of Huawei equipment in the US and pressed other countries to drop Huawei from their telecommunications networks, saying China could use its equipment for espionage.
The indictment covers alleged wrongdoing between about 1999 and 2020.
It accuses Huawei of using Skycom to obtain embargoed US goods, technology and services for Huawei's Iran-based business, and to move money out of that country through the international banking system.
The US said one bank, which was not named in the indictment but which sources and documents reviewed by Reuters identified as HSBC, cleared more than $100 million worth of US-dollar transactions related to Skycom.
Prosecutors accused Meng of misrepresenting Huawei's ownership and control of Skycom in a presentation to an HSBC executive. She later admitted the statements were false, as part of an agreement with prosecutors to drop the charges against her.

articles.title: Inside Russia’s Secret War Games Where Generals Seized Gotland and Defeated NATO
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Inside Russia’s Secret War Games Where Generals Seized Gotland and Defeated NATO
Russian military commanders spent years using large-scale computer simulations to rehearse potential wars with NATO, Sweden, Japan, the US, and Ukraine, including scenarios involving the seizure of Sweden’s Gotland island and operations in the Baltic region.
According to an investigation by the Dossier Center, a Russian investigative media outlet, published on September 8, Russia’s General Staff conducted the simulations at the Military Academy of the General Staff in Moscow, using specialized software to model terrain, military units, weapons, and the actions of opposing forces.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The exercises involved senior Russian officers and, in some cases, more than 1,000 participants connected from military institutions across the country. Officers were divided into opposing teams, while instructors familiar with NATO doctrine frequently represented the adversary.
In one scenario conducted in 2017, Russian commanders modeled operations involving Gotland, a strategically located Swedish island in the Baltic Sea, with Russia’s Kaliningrad region playing an important role in the simulated campaign.
A year later, the Russian military reportedly conducted another simulation involving a fictional war against the US and Japan. More than 320,000 virtual troops were involved, with maps showing areas of northern Japan where key US and Japanese military facilities are located.
Simulating war with Ukraine
The investigation found that Ukraine increasingly became a focus of Russian military simulations ahead of the full-scale invasion. In 2021, Russian commanders reportedly conducted exercises related to a potential operation against Ukraine almost every month.
The simulations relied on a group of interconnected systems developed by Russian defense contractor RusBITech. One platform, Iris-T, generated three-dimensional battlefields using military maps, aerial photography, and satellite imagery. Another system, Spektr-7E, allowed commanders to develop operational plans, simulate their execution, calculate outcomes, and repeat scenarios with different decisions.
By 2021, Spektr-7E reportedly contained around 5,000 digital models representing weapons, military equipment, units, and other objects.
The effectiveness of such simulations, however, depends heavily on the assumptions and intelligence used to construct them. The Dossier Center investigation suggested that inaccurate assessments of Ukraine’s military capabilities and Russia’s own forces may have shaped the scenarios examined by Russian commanders before February 2022.
Russia’s initial attempt to rapidly seize Kyiv and force a political collapse failed after the launch of the full-scale invasion, forcing the Russian military to reconsider some of its operational assumptions.
Russia reworked its war games after 2022
The General Staff subsequently incorporated lessons from the actual fighting in Ukraine into new simulations.
In spring 2022, Russian military institutions held two major command-and-staff exercises. One, completed on April 4, involved nearly 1,300 students and instructors from 15 military educational institutions, according to the investigation.
Later simulations reflected battlefield conditions encountered in Ukraine, including fragmented front lines, special operations forces, foreign fighters, and cities that remained under Ukrainian control behind attempted Russian advances.
The investigation found that Russia continued updating its military gaming system as the war progressed, using battlefield experience to revise scenarios at the General Staff Academy’s military gaming center.
Ukraine and NATO have also expanded their use of war games since Russia’s full-scale invasion. Ukrainian and Western officers have used simulations to examine planned operations, including preparations related to Ukraine’s 2022 counteroffensive in the Kherson region and its 2023 southern offensive.
Ukraine’s battlefield experience is also being incorporated into NATO planning through joint initiatives, including the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC) in Bydgoszcz, Poland, which studies lessons from Russia’s war and integrates them into allied training and planning.

articles.title: A Russian drone hit a Kyiv television newsroom in broad daylight while the channel was live on air
articles.body:
A Russian strike drone hit the Kyiv premises of the television channels My-Ukraina and My-Ukraina+ in the middle of the day on 8 September, the channel reported. The main blow landed on the newsroom and the working offices while My-Ukraina was live on the national newscast. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged a response from Europe and the world.
During its ongoing all-out war, Russia runs a parallel campaign against the people who document it, jailing reporters as terrorists in the territory it occupies, killing them with drones near the front, and accumulating hundreds of crimes against them that European bodies have counted.
The strike landed on the editorial floor
My-Ukraina was broadcasting the national United News telethon, the joint wartime newscast that Ukrainian channels share, at the moment of the attack. Rescuers and medics worked at the site and treated the injured, the channel said. The strike came in daylight, hours after a mass overnight assault on the capital.
Fire and structural destruction hit the business center in the Solomianskyi district, and rescuers evacuated two people from its upper floors, the State Emergency Service said. It put the number injured at five and called that figure preliminary, with the count of victims still being clarified.
"A new page of Russian degradation"
Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that Russia had struck at media and at journalists with a Shahed, one of the Iranian-designed attack drones it launches at Ukrainian cities in mass waves.
"Right in the middle of the day. Exactly when the journalists were on air. The building is partly destroyed," he said.
Emergency workers had already put out the fire, and the number of injured could still grow, he added.
"Shaheds against media is a new page of Russian degradation, and there must certainly be a reaction from Europe and the world," Zelenskyy said.
Trump’s peace envoys left, and Russia hit Kyiv with ballistics—the one thing Ukraine still struggles to stop
Russia had already damaged the channel's office overnight on 20 August during a mass attack on Kyiv. That blast blew out the windows, badly damaged the newsroom, and tore down part of the ceiling in the corridors.
Three killed in the capital over the day
Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said the number of people killed by Russian strikes in Kyiv since the start of 8 September had reached three. The city military administration put the number of injured across the capital at 19.
Explosions ran for almost five hours overnight and damaged more than 50 sites in Kyiv, the Interior Ministry reported. Russia fired ballistic, cruise, and anti-ship missiles along with jet-powered drones in that attack.

articles.title: ‘God Willing, There Will Be a Result’: Zelensky Expects Trump Meeting in September
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky expects to meet US President Donald Trump in the second half of September, where he plans to press Washington for support for Ukraine’s new missile program and supplies of US ballistic missiles.
“I expect to meet with Trump in the second half of September. To raise this issue. And God willing, there will be a result,” Zelensky told journalists, including Kyiv Post, on Tuesday, Sept. 8.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zelensky said Ukraine is developing its “Freya” missile program and hopes the US will support the initiative.
He said Kyiv expects to achieve its desired results with European partners but needs US ballistic missile packages to advance the program.
The meeting could take place on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, where Zelensky has proposed holding a new round of talks involving the United States in late September.
The expected meeting comes amid an intensification of US diplomacy aimed at reviving peace talks. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled from Moscow to Kyiv over the weekend, meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday before holding talks with Zelensky in Kyiv on Sunday.
Witkoff described the discussions with Putin as constructive and said Washington had heard “new ideas” from Moscow, while Kushner referred to a broader “peace package.”
Zelensky called his talks with the US envoys “very substantial” and said Kyiv was ready to move toward trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, the US and Russia. National security advisers from Britain, France and Germany also joined part of the Kyiv discussions.
175 Targets Down, But Ballistic Missiles Still Get Through
Zelensky also said Kyiv and Washington are working toward a trilateral negotiating format.
“We agreed with the American side: let’s prepare all this among ourselves first, and then communicate it publicly,” he said.
The US is also reportedly examining the possibility of a winter de-escalation of the war between Russia and Ukraine alongside renewed negotiations on a broader peace agreement.
Ideas under discussion reportedly include measures involving energy infrastructure, grain supplies, and oil and gas exports.
Envoys say Russia willing to talk
The US delegation visiting Kyiv on Sunday reportedly conveyed to Zelensky that Moscow is prepared to engage in negotiations, even as Russia increases its aggression against Ukraine, casting heavy doubt on that possibility.
Regardless, the meetings appear to have moved forward, as demonstrated by all three sides on Monday.
Witkoff confirmed “substantive progress” had been made, “including movement on scheduling additional trilateral talks.”
Zelensky echoed the development by saying that Ukraine was planning its “next steps” following three rounds of negotiations in Kyiv; and – though offering no timeline for the meetings – the Kremlin said that Moscow did not rule out resuming the trilateral format.

FSB says it detained suspect in attempted murder of Russian general. Ukraine accuses the general of ordering the strike on Kyiv’s Okhmatdyt children’s hospital.
Officers with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) and the country’s federal investigative authority detained a 21-year-old Moldovan citizen, Nicolae Kochu, in the Astrakhan region on suspicion of attempting to murder a Russian serviceman in the Saratov region, the agencies reported.
According to official data, the suspect fired six shots at the serviceman on September 3 in the village of Probuzhdeniye, in the Saratov region’s Engels district. The serviceman was wounded but survived; his name has not been disclosed. The FSB specified only that he holds a high-ranking military position.
Unofficial reports identify him as Major General Nikolai Varpakhovich, commander of the 22nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Division in the long-range aviation branch of Russia’s Aerospace Forces. Ukraine considers him responsible for the missile strike that hit the children’s hospital Okhmatdyt in Kyiv on July 8, 2024, when the facility had more than 600 patients and roughly as many staff members on-site. Two people died in that strike.
The FSB claimed that a Ukrainian intelligence officer recruited Kochu through social media in 2025, while he was looking for work in Moldova. He underwent “mine-explosives and firearms training in Kyiv” in 2026 and traveled to Russia in June with the aim of killing the serviceman.
Kochu was supposed to return to Moldova after the attack, but he was detained while trying to leave Russia. Authorities opened criminal cases against him for attempted murder and illegal arms trafficking.
The FSB released video of Kochu’s detention and questioning, in which he says he saw a job ad on Instagram before Ukrainian representatives contacted him. It is unclear under what circumstances the footage was recorded, and Kochu does not always manage to get his words out on the first try.

articles.title: Foreign components manufactured in 2025-2026 found in Russian Geran drones, Iskander missiles – Vlasiuk
articles.body:
Foreign components manufactured in 2025-2026 found in Russian Geran drones, Iskander missiles – Vlasiuk
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the President's Commissioner for Sanctions Policy, said this in a comment to Ukrinform.
"More strikes, Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones. Their electronic supply chain remains international, and components are still accessible. For example, 96 foreign components were identified in a Geran-4 drone shot down in the Kyiv region on August 12, 2026," he said.
According to the commissioner, these include components manufactured in the United States, China, Taiwan, Germany, Switzerland and Canada by companies including Texas Instruments, Amphenol, Diodes Incorporated, Kyocera AVX, Kemet, ON Semiconductor and Vishay Intertechnology. Seven of the components were manufactured in 2026 and another three in 2025.
"In the Iskander-M missile found at the site of a strike in the Kyiv region in early July, the picture is even broader. A total of 147 foreign-made components were identified. They came from the United States, Belarus, Switzerland, Germany, China and Japan. The manufacturers include Texas Instruments, Analog Devices, Maxim Integrated, Cypress, STMicroelectronics, Macronix, Integrated Silicon Solution, MaxLinear and others. At least 21 components were manufactured in 2025, and there are also components from 2026," he said.
At the same time, Vlasiuk said an examination of the Zarya-61 onboard computer in a Kinzhal missile showed that in 2023 Russia had been replacing U.S.-made Texas Instruments processors with domestically produced chips.
"But in a newer Zarya-61 unit recovered from a missile shot down in May this year, that replacement is no longer there. American processors are being used again. The examination directly indicates that the Russian substitutes did not deliver the required results," he said.
Vlasiuk also highlighted the composition of the computer. A circuit board assembled in May 2025 contains components manufactured in different years, from 2021 to 2024. Among them are a U.S.-made Texas Instruments DSP processor and memory manufactured by IDT, a company now owned by Japan's Renesas. Another board contains a Texas Instruments processor marked with the year 1986 and AMD chips manufactured in 1996.
According to him, this indicates that Russia may use older foreign electronics if they remain suitable for a particular weapons system, while simultaneously incorporating newer components.
"Therefore, the problem for Russia is not a complete lack of domestic electronic components. The same Iskander-M contains 36 Russian-made components and 11 from Belarus. But this is not enough for Russia's sophisticated weapons systems. It has to combine its domestic component base with foreign-made components, sourcing them through different markets and supply chains. Every manufacturer, law enforcement agency and export-control authority has enough information to stop such supplies to Russia," Vlasiuk added.

articles.title: Exclusive: Iraqi factions reject September weapons deadline
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Iraqi factions reject September deadline to hand over weapons
Two prominent Iran-aligned Iraqi armed factions have told The New Arab they will not hand over their weapons by a government-imposed deadline at the end of September unless Baghdad meets a series of conditions, including the withdrawal of US and Turkish forces from the country.
In exclusive comments to The New Arab, spokesmen for the Sayyid al-Shuhada Brigades and the Nujaba Movement said they did not consider the 30 September deadline binding and would not disarm in return for promises that failed to guarantee Iraq's security and sovereignty.
Sheikh Kadhim al-Fartousi, spokesman for the Sayyid al-Shuhada Brigades, said the group would not hand over its weapons within the government-set deadline unless conditions previously communicated to negotiating parties affiliated with the Coordination Framework were met.
Speaking to The New Arab in Baghdad on Monday, around three weeks before the deadline, Al-Fartousi said the group's position had been made clear during talks between armed factions and Coordination Framework representatives over the previous two days.
"The Brigades refuse to hand over their weapons within the deadline set by the Iraqi government unless the conditions it previously announced are met," he said.
"This position was clearly conveyed to the negotiating parties affiliated with the Coordination Framework during the talks held with armed factions over the past two days."
Al-Fartousi said the Brigades and other armed factions within the "Axis of Resistance" continued to "insist on the need for a vision that guarantees Iraq's security and sovereignty".
"We affirm that strengthening the authority of the state and placing weapons under the control of its institutions cannot be achieved separately from addressing the challenges and threats that the factions believe still exist," he said.
Al-Fartousi said the factions supported strengthening state authority and regulating weapons but argued that their conditions must first be met to ensure Iraq could defend itself against external threats.
He also said the factions did not trust promises that US forces would fully withdraw from Iraq, arguing that previous withdrawal announcements had not ended the presence or movement of US forces in the country.
"The position of the Brigades and the other factions is not based on rejecting the strengthening of the state's authority, but rather on the need to provide conditions that guarantee the state can exercise its sovereignty and its ability to protect its territory and airspace," he said.
The factions' main demands include the withdrawal of US and Turkish forces from Iraq, an end to what they describe as Washington's "political and financial tutelage", the dismantling of the Peshmerga and deployment of federal forces in the Kurdistan Region, and the provision of missile and air defence systems capable of protecting Iraqi airspace.
Mehdi al-Kaabi, a leader in the Nujaba Movement, separately told The New Arab that his group also "does not regard the government deadline for handing over weapons as binding".
"Any talk of handing over weapons before the conditions previously announced by the factions are met is meaningless," Al-Kaabi said.
He said the factions rejected what he described as a unilateral process in which they would be required to relinquish their weapons without guarantees that Iraq could protect its territory and sovereignty.
"Weapons are not the problem in themselves, but rather the problem is Iraq remaining exposed to foreign forces and external attacks," he said.
Al-Kaabi said any process to regulate weapons must be preceded by the withdrawal of US and Turkish forces and measures to strengthen the state's ability to protect its territory and airspace.
He said the factions "will not accept handing over their weapons in exchange for promises or unsecured timetables", arguing that placing weapons under state control must be accompanied by guarantees that foreign forces cannot operate in Iraqi territory or airspace without approval.
"The factions support a strong state that possesses its security and military decision-making," Al-Kaabi said, but "will not be a party to arrangements that weaken Iraq's deterrence capabilities or strip it of its means of defence".
The Sayyid al-Shuhada Brigades and Nujaba are among several armed factions resisting the government's timetable, alongside Hezbollah Brigades and al-Awfiya.
The Iraqi government set 30 September as the deadline for bringing weapons outside official institutions under state control, warning that "any weapons remaining outside state authority after this date will be subject to legal action".
The government has said it wants to resolve the issue through dialogue rather than confrontation and maintains that the remaining disagreement centres largely on how and when weapons are brought under state control.

articles.title: Syria’s Assad-era reactor configured for nuclear weapons: IAEA
articles.body:
Syria’s Assad-era reactor configured for nuclear weapons: IAEA
UN watchdog says material now is under IAEA safeguards.
Syria’s Assad-era nuclear facility was configured to produce material for possible use in nuclear weapons, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency has reported.
The nuclear reactor, which the United Nations nuclear watchdog has been investigating with the cooperation of Syria’s new authorities, would have been able to produce fissile material that could be used for weapons, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told a media conference in Vienna on Monday.
“This is a reactor that is very efficient in the production of fissile material that could be used directly for the fabrication of nuclear weapons,” he said.
Grossi’s comments came a week after the UN watchdog revealed in a confidential report that it had visited several sites in Syria in August and carried out verification work.
Based on observations at the Deir Az Zor site, the agency said it confirms “that the cooling infrastructure which has now been uncovered is consistent with that of a nuclear reactor”.
The agency added that it would continue to monitor the activities at the site “as the excavation work progresses”.
Syria was believed to have operated an extensive, undeclared nuclear programme under former President Bashar al-Assad that included a nuclear reactor built by North Korea in Deir Az Zor.
It only became public knowledge after Israeli air strikes in 2007 destroyed the facility. Syria later levelled the site and never responded fully to the IAEA’s questions about it.
Grossi said when the inspectors visited the site in August they had to “tear down walls” and go through “very difficult and narrow passages” to reach the nuclear material that had been hidden. The site had “boxes scattered all over the place,” he said.
Grossi said that “the important thing is that this material now is under safeguards” of the IAEA, adding that agency inspectors had managed to install cameras there.
Israel is believed to have its own undeclared atomic weapons programme, which makes it the only nuclear armed country in the Middle East. Israel neither confirms nor denies having nuclear weapons.
The IAEA has said that the former Syrian authorities had failed to report nuclear material, facilities and activities.
Besides the nuclear reactor at Deir Az Zor, the IAEA listed a fuel fabrication plant, where nuclear fuel for the reactor was manufactured and a store for the nuclear fuel, uranium scrap and waste.
During the visit to Syria last month, an IAEA team also visited a previously undeclared site.
The Syrian administration – made up of the group that overthrew Assad in 2024 – notified the agency of its existence in July and invited the nuclear inspectors to investigate.

articles.title: Russia burns occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant’s last-resort generators as everyday power, Ukraine says
articles.body:
The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant lost the 330-kV Ferosplavna-1 line—which the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) called the plant's only remaining off-site power line—on 20 August and has since run on emergency diesel generators, Ukraine's state nuclear operator Energoatom said on 6 September. A day earlier, the IAEA said the plant's diesel reserves were under increasing strain and warned it could lose all power within days unless external power was restored or fuel deliveries continued.
The Zaporizhzhia plant has been under Russian control since March 2022, when Russian forces seized the facility during the invasion. The plant stopped generating electricity in September 2022, and all six reactors have been in cold shutdown since April 2024, leaving the plant dependent on external or backup power for cooling and other essential safety systems. Repeated damage to the plant's external power connections has forced it onto emergency diesel generators multiple times, including during a month-long loss of off-site power in 2025.
How much diesel the Zaporizhzhia plant has left
The plant's most recent delivery to its off-site fuel farm took place in March, and the next one, set for May, is still held up by military activity, the IAEA reported on 20 August. At that point, the plant reported having more than 10 days of diesel available for its emergency generators.
By 29 August, the plant was down to about 10 days of diesel—its minimum regulatory reserve—and IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said that was roughly how long it had left without restored power or more deliveries. Several dozen tons reached the plant on 27 and 28 August, but a week later the agency shortened the warning to within days, with the plant down to two generators and running its cooling pumps on and off to save fuel. No nuclear plant should have to throttle its essential cooling systems to conserve diesel, Grossi said.
How the plant lost its last external power line
Ferosplavna-1 is a backup line from the thermal plant next door, one of 10 the IAEA counted before the war. The main 750-kV Dniprovska line failed on 24 March. Technicians repaired it under a June ceasefire, but it has never been switched back on, because a substation more than 100 kilometers away was badly damaged. Ferosplavna-1 has carried the plant alone since. It went down on 26 April for the 15th time since 2022, by both counts, and cut out repeatedly around a June attack on the thermal plant. It went dead on 20 August—the 27th loss by Energoatom's count, the 26th by the IAEA's.
Ukrainian technicians began repairs on 5 September under a local ceasefire the IAEA brokered, with a few days' work expected. The line was still dead on 7 September, its 19th day without off-site power, the plant's Russian-installed management claimed to Russian media. Fixing it may not bring the power back anyway, Rosatom chief Aleksei Likhachev claimed the same day, blaming Ukrainian inaction for the other line still sitting repaired and unconnected—which the IAEA puts down to the wrecked substation.
Energoatom's assessment of the generator risk and Russian claims
Russian forces run the plant's emergency generators as everyday power, outside the conditions they were built for, Energoatom said on 6 September. Weeks of continuous running raise the risk of several backups failing together, and constant starts under load make the systems that start them likelier to fail. Even in cold shutdown, a blackout would threaten control of the safety systems and the spent fuel pools, and the plant is already in gross violation of its safe-operation limits, it said. Only a Russian pullout, military and civilian, and a handover back to Energoatom would guarantee safe operation, the company said, which also wants both grid lines back.
The plant has enough fuel for its generators but cannot restock while the access roads are shelled, the plant's Russian-installed management claimed to Russia's state news agency TASS on 31 August. TASS blamed Ukrainian forces for the shelling, though the quoted remarks named no one.

articles.title: UK allocates over €100m winter air defence package for Ukraine, including Patriot missiles
articles.body:
UK allocates over €100m winter air defence package for Ukraine, including Patriot missiles
The United Kingdom is providing £100 million (around €116 million) for an air defence package for Ukraine ahead of winter, including Patriot missiles. The weapons will be supplied through the PURL mechanism, a US-NATO initiative under which European NATO allies purchase American weapons for Ukraine.
Source: European Pravda, citing the UK government
Details: As part of the new package, the UK will provide air defence interceptors, large-calibre artillery shells and drones to help Ukraine defend itself against Russian attacks this winter.
The weapons will be supplied through the PURL mechanism, under which Ukraine's allies purchase US weapons for its needs.
The Patriot missiles and other air defence equipment will be delivered to Ukraine before winter sets in, helping it protect critical national infrastructure, civilians and its armed forces from Russian attacks.
The aid announcement follows visits to Kyiv by the UK prime minister and defence secretary, who heard from the Ukrainian president about the importance of additional support ahead of winter.
"Both the Prime Minister and I heard loud and clear on our first visits to Kyiv the importance of supporting Ukraine through this winter, as Putin prepares to use winter as a weapon by continuing barbaric attacks against civilian and energy targets. We promised to mobilise allies and provide more support wherever we can," Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said.
Background:
- On 8 September, Streeting is chairing his first meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group (also known as the Ramstein format), the 50-country alliance providing military equipment to Ukraine. The 36th Ramstein meeting is taking place remotely, co-chaired by the UK and German defence ministers.
- On 7 September, an extraordinary meeting of the NATO-Ukraine Council at the level of permanent representatives took place at NATO headquarters in Brussels, during which Ukraine presented a list of its priority and urgent needs for air and missile defence systems.

articles.title: The economic risks of a Gulf tanker war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
As Gulf crisis morphs to tanker war, what are the economic implications?
The escalating conflict in the Strait of Hormuz is beginning to pose a much bigger question for Gulf economies: how long can their enormous financial reserves shield them from a prolonged disruption to one of the world's most important energy routes?
For now, countries including the UAE, Qatar and Kuwait have formidable financial defences. But analysts warn that even those buffers have limits if the crisis stretches into 2027.
Fitch Ratings has warned that “rating risks for some issuers in Gulf Cooperation Council countries could increase under a hypothetical scenario in which passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted through most of 2027”.
The agency said the “extremely large sovereign financial buffers in Kuwait, the UAE and Qatar have been a key factor in limiting the conflict’s impact on credit ratings”. But the longer the disruption continues, the more those reserves risk being drawn down to compensate for falling exports, higher shipping and insurance costs, and wider economic damage.
Firas Shaabo, professor of financial management at Istanbul’s Başakşehir University, says the immediate problem is not whether Gulf states have enough money. It is the accumulating “cost of the shock”.
Sovereign wealth funds give governments considerable room to absorb the impact, he says, but that protection is temporary rather than unlimited.
The warning comes as the confrontation at sea has sharply intensified. US Central Command announced that it had targeted three Iranian oil tankers, including one near Kharg Island, after Iran's Revolutionary Guard launched ballistic missiles towards two US warships.
The IRGC subsequently said it had targeted three tankers which, according to its account, were travelling along unauthorised routes through Hormuz, as well as three vessels linked to the United States.
The result is a rapidly deteriorating environment for shipping, insurance and trade finance - and Gulf economies are among the most exposed. Two large tankers carrying Saudi crude were attacked almost simultaneously as they left the Strait of Hormuz on 31 August.
The Saudi tanker Sadr and the Liberia-flagged Senegal Prosperity were each carrying about two million barrels of crude. Saudi Arabia's National Shipping Company, Bahri, later said two Filipino crew members aboard the Sadr had been killed.
By 2 September, the International Maritime Organization had recorded 72 confirmed incidents targeting international shipping in the region, with 21 seafarers killed.
Shipping slows to a trickle
The scale of the disruption can already be seen in vessel movements. Kpler data showed only five commercial ships passing through Hormuz last Saturday. None were recorded crossing on Sunday.
That compared with 31 vessels during the previous weekend. Traffic remained in single digits at the beginning of September, as large oil and gas carriers increasingly avoided the strait.
For Gulf exporters, that matters because Hormuz is not simply a shipping route. For several states, it is the principal outlet through which their energy exports reach international markets.
Saudi Arabia has some ability to bypass it through infrastructure connecting its oil industry to the Red Sea. Other Gulf states have far fewer alternatives.
Fitch said financial reserves would continue to provide substantial protection under a prolonged-conflict scenario, but warned that extended disruption could eventually damage the credit profiles of states without alternative export routes such as pipelines bypassing Hormuz.
The effect is being amplified by extraordinary increases in insurance costs. War-risk premiums for crude tankers have risen from about 0.25% of a vessel's value before the confrontation to between 7.5% and 12.5% in August.
For shipowners, that can make voyages commercially unattractive. Operators must either absorb enormous additional costs, pass them on through higher freight rates or avoid the region altogether.
When large reserves are not enough
The Gulf states are often portrayed as possessing almost inexhaustible financial resources because of the size of their sovereign wealth funds. But Shaabo says that can be misleading.
Those funds are not vast pools of cash that governments can immediately deploy. Their holdings range from relatively small amounts of liquid reserves, to investments that can be sold quickly but potentially at a loss during turbulent markets, and large portfolios of long-term assets that cannot easily be converted into cash.
The important question, therefore, is not simply how large a country's sovereign wealth fund is. It is how much immediately accessible liquidity it has - and how long that liquidity can sustain government spending and economic support if the disruption continues.
That distinction becomes increasingly important if the Hormuz crisis moves from a temporary shock to a persistent economic problem. A prolonged disruption could weaken growth and government revenues at the same time as states face higher spending requirements.
Eventually, Shaabo warns, that combination could begin affecting sovereign creditworthiness.
Higher oil prices offer only partial protection. They may increase the value of every barrel Gulf producers are able to export, helping compensate for some losses.
But higher prices matter much less if exporters cannot physically move the same quantities of crude. Restricted export routes mean lower volumes, while transport, insurance and import costs rise sharply.
The result could be weaker economic activity even as headline oil prices remain high.
Iran has added to that uncertainty by expanding the number of vessels on its blacklist in the strait to 56 on 2 September. The list includes oil tankers and carriers of liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas.
Iran has threatened listed vessels with fines, seizure or detention, and warned that action could also be taken against ships conducting ship-to-ship cargo transfers with them, according to Reuters.
A crisis extending beyond oil
The risks are also spreading into the financial and legal machinery underpinning international trade. The continuing turmoil has exposed weaknesses in insurance contracts used by lenders and charterers to finance shipments.
Some war-risk clauses may not have been designed for a crisis developing at the current pace. That creates uncertainty over who carries the financial risk when vessels are prevented from sailing or when routes suddenly become too dangerous.
Ship charter agreements can also limit an owner's ability to avoid areas formally designated as war-risk zones. According to Lloyd's List, the result could be prolonged contractual disputes, higher litigation costs and reduced availability of trade finance.
That means the impact of the Hormuz confrontation does not stop with oil tankers. It can gradually spread through banks, insurers, shipping companies, importers and government finances.
Three possible paths
Shaabo sees three broad scenarios. The first - and in his view currently the least likely - is a relatively rapid settlement followed by the gradual resumption of shipping.
Under that scenario, Gulf governments could rely on reserves, additional borrowing and adjustments to spending without putting their sovereign ratings under serious pressure.
The second is considerably more damaging. If disruption lasts several months, what begins as a shipping and logistics crisis could develop into a wider financial and economic problem.
Growth could slow as inflation and government spending rise. Capital could leave the region, bank profits could decline and major investments in transport, logistics, tourism and property could be delayed.
Governments would then face an increasingly difficult choice between maintaining spending and subsidies, depleting financial assets or taking on substantially more debt.
The third scenario is the most severe. Shaabo estimates a 20% to 25% probability of sustained physical damage to infrastructure including oil facilities, ports, refineries, pipelines and power stations.
At that point, the nature of the crisis changes. It would no longer simply be a question of temporarily preventing Gulf states from exporting what they produce.
Their ability to produce energy itself could be reduced. Sovereign wealth funds are far less effective against that kind of shock because the problem becomes a loss of future income rather than a temporary shortage of cash.
That could lead directly to negative reviews of sovereign credit ratings.
Not all Gulf states face the same risk
The impact would also be highly uneven. Economic expert and financial adviser Ali Ahmed Darwish says the Fitch warning should be treated with particular seriousness because the crisis highlights significant differences between Gulf economies.
Saudi Arabia has the advantage of alternative export infrastructure towards the Red Sea. For states whose geography leaves them overwhelmingly dependent on Hormuz, the options are much narrower.
Those countries may eventually have to undertake far-reaching changes to their supply and export networks. But alternative routes can be extremely expensive, technically difficult or simply impractical.
Darwish argues that governments will therefore also need to make greater use of partnerships with the private sector, particularly banks. Banks could work with insurers and reinsurers to maintain trade credit and contain the rapidly rising cost of maritime insurance.
That could reduce the pressure on governments to continually draw on sovereign funds or seek additional external financing. But there is a limit to how long these measures can compensate for a fundamental disruption to trade.
If the war and interruption to shipping continue into 2027, Darwish says Gulf states could face a genuine challenge in meeting financial obligations and preserving monetary stability.
Kareem Ramadan is a Muscat-based correspondent for The New Arab's Arabic edition, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed.

articles.title: Ukrainian company unveils RAM-2X strike drone for first time, used to hit over 450 targets – photo, video
articles.body:
Ukrainian company unveils RAM-2X strike drone for first time, used to hit over 450 targets – photo, video
Ukrainian company Ukrspecsystems, which develops reconnaissance and strike drones, has publicly unveiled its RAM-2X strike UAV with an X-shaped wing for the first time. The drone was presented at the MSPO defence exhibition in Poland.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda
Details: The RAM-2X was designed to strike high-value targets at ranges of up to 180 km. The drone can remain airborne for more than two hours and has a high degree of automation. It can carry a 2.7 kg or 3.5 kg explosively formed penetrator warhead.
"Each type of equipment performs its own task, and every target requires an appropriate means of engagement. Following a comprehensive approach, we are developing strike systems in several subclasses at once, built around standardised components, a common ground station and unified software," Ukrspecsystems representatives said.
The RAM-2X can also use various AI assistant models to improve its effectiveness and operate with different communications systems. The drone can use several radio-frequency bands or Starlink.
In addition, the RAM-2X can operate together with a SHARK-M reconnaissance UAV acting as a communications relay. In this configuration, the reconnaissance drone provides targeting data and helps overcome enemy electronic warfare systems.
Ukrspecsystems says RAM loitering munitions have struck more than 450 targets. Although footage of these drones being used in combat has regularly appeared in the public domain, the company was unable for a long time to publicly confirm its connection to RAM due to security restrictions.
Ukrspecsystems has now decided to open its own "X-Files", a series of publications featuring footage of the drones being used in combat. The first compilation focuses on strikes against Russian air defence systems. Its publication was approved by the military.
RAM-2X drone strikes on targets. Video: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine
"These are targets that are themselves designed to hunt drones. There are simply no more difficult targets for a strike drone. Secondly, because of their value, they are better camouflaged and positioned further from the front line. That is why striking an air defence system or radar demonstrates the key capabilities: the system's ability to overcome electronic warfare and enemy defences and operate far beyond the line of contact," Ukrspecsystems representatives explained, describing why they chose to publish footage of strikes on air defence systems first.
Background: Ukrspecsystems previously announced that it had developed a ready-to-use medium-range strike drone similar to the US Hornet.

articles.title: The broken illusion: US fails to subdue Iran in war
articles.body:
A war becomes a victory for a great power when it can achieve the objectives it set for starting it; inflicting damage or carrying out extensive attacks alone is not a sign of victory. Now, the more time passes since the start of America's war against Iran, the more the gap between the victory narrative in Washington and the reality on the ground becomes apparent.
America's failed war against Iran has gradually turned into a domestic issue in the United States. What was initially supposed to be a display of Washington's power and proof of its ability to impose its will on Tehran is now facing serious questions about the human, military, and economic costs of the war. Under such circumstances, opposition to the Trump administration's policies is no longer raised only by foreign critics, but a number of American politicians are also warning about the results of this war.
Chris Murphy, the Democratic senator from Connecticut, pointing to the consequences of the war against Iran, has presented a picture of the costs that, according to him, the United States has incurred as a result of this conflict. Murphy announced that 18 Americans have been killed, billions of dollars in damage have been inflicted on US bases, and the country's missile stockpiles have been severely depleted. He also pointed to the economic pressures on American farmers and the rise in gasoline prices to around five dollars; an issue that shows the consequences of the war no longer remain confined to military bases and the battlefield, but have spread into the daily lives of American society.
But the most important part of Murphy's remarks is not his reference to casualties and damages, but his assessment of Iran's situation. The American senator has stressed that Iran is "stronger than ever" and that Trump, in contrast, has become dangerously delusional. These words in effect constitute a direct blow to the US government's narrative about the outcome of the war; a narrative that tries to present extensive military strikes as equivalent to victory.
The main problem with this narrative is that victory in war cannot be measured solely by the number of attacks, the amount of bombs used, or the damage inflicted on the opposing side's infrastructure. The real criterion is the achievement of political and military objectives. If the goal of the war was to weaken Iran, destroy its capacity for resistance, and force Tehran to accept Washington's demands, then Iran's continued ability to confront, respond, and rebuild its capacities shows that these objectives have not been achieved.
On the other hand, the United States has paid considerable costs to continue this war. The depletion of missile stockpiles, increased pressure on military bases, American casualties, and the economic effects of the war are all part of the cost Washington must pay to continue the conflict. These costs become even more significant when the opposing side still retains the ability to continue the war. In a war of attrition, the issue is not only who has inflicted more damage; the decisive question is who has greater capacity to absorb the blows and keep going.
This is where Trump's claim of victory faces a serious challenge. The US government can speak of the success of military operations and the damage inflicted on Iran, but if these operations have not been able to deter Tehran from continuing its resistance, the final result will fall far short of the classic definition of victory. Military victory must ultimately lead to a lasting political achievement; otherwise, large-scale attacks may simply turn into a cycle of attrition that imposes costs on both sides.
From this very perspective, Murphy's remarks gain greater significance. He is effectively drawing the attention of American public opinion away from images of attacks and displays of military power toward the bill for the war. A bill that includes human casualties, the consumption of weapons stockpiles, damage to bases, economic pressure, and the rising cost of living for the American people. When such costs are set alongside the failure to achieve the war's primary objectives, the question about the real success of these operations becomes unavoidable.
In this context, the claim that "Iran has become stronger" should also be examined within the same framework. Power does not mean merely an increase in the number of military equipment. The ability to maintain political cohesion, continue economic activity, rebuild defensive capacities, preserve the ability to respond, and most importantly, prevent the enemy from imposing its political will are all part of a country's power in wartime. If Iran, after enduring heavy attacks, still retains the ability to continue the confrontation, this in itself shows that the American strategy has not been able to achieve the result for which it was designed.
In contrast, the United States also faces an important issue: prolonged wars carry costs for Washington far beyond military operations. They consume weapons stockpiles, put forces and equipment at risk, create economic pressure, and can ultimately deepen the political divide within the United States. The longer the war drags on, the more serious this question becomes: whether its achievements have been worth such a cost.
For this reason, the war against Iran cannot be assessed solely through images of attacks and official American statements. The reality on the ground becomes clear when the stated objectives are compared with the actual results. If the United States, despite using its enormous military capacity, has not been able to force Iran to surrender, has not been able to eliminate its capacity for resistance, and has simultaneously faced casualties, depleted weapons stockpiles, and economic pressure, then speaking of victory will be difficult.
America has lost this war; not only because of the heavy costs, but because it has not been able to achieve its primary objectives. The more important issue is that this failure is no longer raised only in the analyses of Washington's opponents. Now the voice of criticism is also being heard from within the American political structure, and politicians like Chris Murphy are warning about the gap between the war's costs and its achievements.
Ultimately, what is collapsing today more than anything else is not just a military strategy, but the illusion of an easy American victory against Iran; an illusion that imagined a country could be forced to surrender through firepower. The reality of the war, however, has shown that real power is not limited to the ability to attack; sometimes more important than that is the ability to stand, to respond, and to keep going. And Iran, at least according to the existing realities, is still standing.
MNA

articles.title: Trump’s Ukraine plans ‘scared Europeans to death’ – Lavrov
articles.body:
Trump’s Ukraine plans ‘scared Europeans to death’ – Lavrov
European leaders were “scared to death” by US President Donald Trump’s proposals for resolving the Ukraine conflict and worked relentlessly to sabotage Washington’s compromise efforts, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
In an interview published on Tuesday, Lavrov accused European NATO members of seeking to prevent Trump from returning to the ideas he had discussed with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Alaska last year. He also pointed to a phone call between the two leaders on July 4 this year.
“Europe understands that if the Americans suddenly return to their original proposals... as was the case in Anchorage, Europe was simply scared to death,” Lavrov said. According to him, European leaders “immediately rushed” to coax Trump into abandoning his own initiatives.
Lavrov recalled French President Emmanuel Macron’s remarks at a NATO summit in June, at which the French leader had effectively boasted that the Anchorage initiative had been “buried” and that Washington was once again aligned with Europe in a united front against Russia.
“If Western diplomacy comes down to restraining countries that put forward reasonable, balanced, compromise initiatives, then so be it,” Lavrov said. Moscow would then pursue its objectives “not at the negotiating table,” which he said Russia would prefer, “but on the battlefield.”
Lavrov’s remarks come as the Trump administration makes a renewed push to revive stalled diplomacy. US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Saturday for more than three hours before traveling on to Kiev the following day.
The White House said the sides discussed “substantive plans for next steps” toward ending the conflict, while Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov described the meeting as “extremely frank” and said the American envoys had presented a number of ideas on possible avenues toward a settlement.
Lavrov, however, argued that most of the public talk about diplomacy coming from Kiev and its Western sponsors is intended to secure another pause in the fighting and give their Ukrainian proxies time to rearm and regroup. Despite the renewed US effort, Lavrov insisted that no constructive peace negotiations are currently under way.
“Nothing is happening on the diplomatic front,” he said, adding that developments are instead unfolding “on the real front,” where Russian forces are advancing.
The foreign minister also warned that Moscow intends to follow through on threats of retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilian infrastructure. Russia had warned that such strikes would trigger a response “much heavier for Ukraine,” he said, adding: “This is happening now.”
The top Russian diplomat also took aim at London, which has vowed to remain with Kiev to the end. “I feel sorry for Britain,” he said, since that end “will not be a happy one.”
Addressing European preparations for a possible future conflict with Moscow, Lavrov reiterated Putin’s position that Russia has no intention of attacking Europe. If European countries were to attack Russia, however, he warned that it would be “a fundamentally different war” and “very short.”
